topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Experimental vs Theoretical
topic.description: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
evidence: Roll a die 60 times and compare experimental frequencies with the expected 10 per number
Explain why experimental results don't exactly match theoretical predictions but get closer with more trials
Predict what would happen if the experiment were repeated 600 times instead of 60
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads, do they understand why this doesn't mean heads is "more likely" — and that the more times you flip, the closer the results get to 50:50?

pedagogy.summary: Experimental vs theoretical bridges the two faces of probability: the theoretical value calculated from equally-likely outcomes, and the experimental value (relative frequency) measured from actual trials. The key idea is the law of large numbers in child form — as the number of trials grows, the experimental probability tends toward the theoretical, while short runs can differ wildly and each trial stays independent. The procedure is to run trials, compute relative frequencies from the data, and compare with prediction.
bestPractices: Have children compute relative frequency from THEIR OWN tally (frequency ÷ trials), not restate the theoretical value
Contrast a short run with a long run — pool class data or use a simulator — so convergence toward theory is seen, not asserted
Name explicitly that closeness improves with MORE trials but exact equality is not expected
Attack the 'due' fallacy directly: the die does not self-correct; relative frequency converges, absolute counts do not equalise exactly
Use the comparison to judge fairness sensibly — a big deviation over many trials suggests bias, a deviation over a few does not
keyRepresentations: Tally / frequency table with a relative-frequency column (f ÷ n)
Relative-frequency line converging toward the theoretical line as trials increase
Short-run vs long-run comparison side by side
Experimental value and theoretical value marked on the same 0-to-1 scale
commonMisconceptions: Expecting experimental results to equal the theoretical probability, and calling a device biased after a short run (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts 'catch up' to become exactly equal with more trials (gambler's fallacy of convergence / the 'due' idea)
Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one (or vice versa)
Trusting a small sample as much as a large one to estimate an unknown probability

learn.summary: Learners compare experimental probability (relative frequency measured from actual trials) with theoretical probability (calculated from equally-likely outcomes). The central idea is a child-level law of large numbers: as the number of trials grows, the experimental relative frequency tends toward the theoretical value, while short runs can differ widely and each trial stays independent. Learners run trials, compute relative frequency from their OWN tally (frequency ÷ number of trials), and compare with prediction — and they confront two common fallacies: that experimental results should equal theory exactly, and that outcomes become 'due' or that absolute counts catch up to be equal.

activities.title: Roll, tally, and compute your own experimental probability
feedback: If a learner writes 1/6 for each outcome without using their tally, point out the task asked for the value from the rolls — re-establish: experimental = from your data (f ÷ n); theoretical = from the equally-likely outcomes.

If a learner calls the die loaded because a number came up 14 times instead of 10 in 60 rolls, acknowledge the deviation is real but note that a deviation of this size over only 60 trials is quite common for a fair die; deciding fairness needs many more trials.
If a learner expects the experimental values to match 1/6 exactly, affirm that close-not-exact is the normal and correct expectation for a fair die over a short run.
activities.rationale: Computing relative frequency from a learner's own data, rather than restating the theoretical value, is what makes the two meanings of probability distinct and exposes whether a learner confuses them. A short run of rolls is not enough to conclude bias, which is why the activity frames the deviation as expected.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.
learnerActions: Roll a die 60 times (or flip a coin / spin a spinner), tallying each result in a frequency table.
Add a relative-frequency column: for each outcome compute frequency ÷ 60 as a fraction or decimal.
State the theoretical probability (1/6 for a fair die) and mark both the experimental and theoretical values on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Write in your own words how your experimental values compare with 1/6, and whether the differences you see are enough to call the die unfair.
activities.intendedInsight: Experimental probability comes from the data you collected (f ÷ n); it is usually close to but not exactly the theoretical value, and ordinary short-run differences are expected rather than proof of bias.

activities.title: Short run vs long run: watch the proportion settle while counts stay unequal
feedback: If a learner predicts exactly 100 of each number in 600 rolls, distinguish relative frequency (approaches 1/6) from raw counts (need not equalise); the proportions converge even though the counts stay unequal.

If a learner says a rarely-rolled number is 'due' to appear, state plainly that the die does not self-correct and each roll is independent — long-run convergence of proportions does not make any single outcome more likely on the next roll.

If a learner links convergence to sample size correctly, confirm that more trials give a more reliable estimate and that this is exactly how you would sensibly judge fairness: a big deviation over MANY trials suggests bias; a deviation over a few does not.
activities.rationale: Seeing a long run (pooled or simulated) lets convergence be observed rather than merely asserted, and displaying raw counts alongside proportions directly targets the gambler's-fallacy belief that counts equalise. Treating recency ('due') errors as a failure of independence is the documented misconception to confront.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.

Recency errors (an outcome is 'due', or a streak will continue) reflect a failure to treat trials as independent, and belief in short-sequence representativeness makes people expect small samples to mirror the theoretical distribution.
learnerActions: Compare your own short run (60 rolls) with a much longer run — pool the whole class's tallies, or use a trials simulator set to 60, then 600, then 6000.
At each trial count, record both the relative frequency for each outcome AND the raw counts.
Predict before increasing the trials: 'If I roll 600 times instead of 60, will each number come up exactly 100 times?' Then check against the data.

Describe what gets closer to what: check whether, at the largest trial count, the relative frequencies for a fair die all sit near 1/6 (or near the theoretical value for your coin or spinner), while the raw counts (for example 995 vs 1020) are still unequal.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the PROPORTION (relative frequency) that converges toward the theoretical value with more trials — not the absolute counts becoming equal. No outcome is ever 'due', and each trial is independent of the ones before it.

activities.title: Judge a fairness claim from sample size
feedback: If a learner concludes bias from 14-out-of-60, redirect to the plan: extend the run or pool more trials, because bias needs many trials to judge and 14 against an expected 10 is within normal short-run variation.
If a learner trusts 20 flips as much as 500, point to the law-of-large-numbers idea: more trials give a more reliable estimate.
Confirm answers that propose collecting many more trials as the way to judge fairness much more reliably, and note that this gives strong evidence, not absolute certainty.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a fairness claim and ordering sample sizes tests the reasoning about MORE trials where the law-of-large-numbers understanding shows. This is interpretation work and does not itself generate the convergence experience, so it complements running trials rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.

Recency errors (an outcome is 'due', or a streak will continue) reflect a failure to treat trials as independent, and belief in short-sequence representativeness makes people expect small samples to mirror the theoretical distribution.
learnerActions: Read a scenario: 'A 4 came up 14 times in 60 rolls of a die.' Decide whether this proves the die is biased, and explain your reasoning.
Decide whose data you would trust more to estimate the chance of an outcome for a possibly-bent coin: 20 flips or 500 flips, and say why.
Order several sample sizes from least to most reliable for estimating an unknown probability.
Explain how you WOULD decide, with much more confidence, whether the die is loaded — and why even many trials give strong evidence rather than absolute certainty.
activities.intendedInsight: A small sample is not as trustworthy as a large one for estimating an unknown probability; a single ordinary deviation over few trials is not evidence of bias, and judging fairness sensibly depends on the number of trials behind the data.

constraints: Learners must compute relative frequency from their OWN tally (frequency ÷ trials), not restate the theoretical value.
Name explicitly that closeness to theory improves with MORE trials but exact equality is not expected — and that it is the proportion that converges, not the counts that equalise.
Confront the 'due' fallacy directly: the die does not self-correct and each trial is independent; relative frequency converges while absolute counts do not equalise exactly.

A multiple-choice or ordering item can assess reading a convergence graph or judging a fairness claim from sample size, but it cannot let a learner run and scale trials — so recognition items should supplement, not replace, actually running experiments.

An interpretation-only or discussion-only activity can analyse convergence but does not itself generate the long-run experience; learners still need to run or pool trials to see the proportion settle.

Optional interactive scaffold: a die/coin/spinner simulator with a slider or buttons for 20, 60, 600, 6000 trials, plotting a live experimental relative-frequency line against the theoretical line plus a raw-count display, makes the convergence mechanism concrete. This is one helpful way to show the effect, not a required mechanism — pooling class tallies serves the same purpose.
Use fairness judgement sensibly: a big deviation over many trials suggests bias; a deviation over a few does not.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source framed a 3D dice-roller as adding 'little' and static images / dialogue as 'poor' because they cannot run trials. The genuine objective limit retained here is only that recognition-only or non-running formats do not themselves generate the long-run convergence experience; claims that extra dimensions 'buy little' or that a static image 'cannot teach this' were catalog preferences and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic and probability logic: for 60 rolls of a fair die the expected count per outcome is 10 (60 × 1/6); experimental relative frequencies are each frequency ÷ 60; theoretical is 1/6 ≈ 0.167. For 600 rolls the expected count is 100 each, but exactly 100 each is NOT expected — only that relative frequencies approach 1/6. These are consistent across the source and reproduced faithfully. The example raw counts (e.g. 995 vs 1020, 980 vs 1015) are illustrative of 'unequal counts at large n' and are plausible for large die runs; they are kept as illustrations, not as guaranteed results.

Independent editor re-audit: no critical learner-facing factual or logic errors were found. The convergence-of-proportions-vs-counts distinction, the independence/'due' framing, and the sample-size reasoning are internally coherent across summary, actions, insights and feedback; the '14 vs expected 10 in 60 rolls' is correctly treated as within normal short-run variation.

probeDeeper: Your 4 came up 14 times, not 10 — does that prove the die is loaded? How could you decide for sure?
If you rolled 600 times, would each number come up exactly 100 times? What exactly gets closer to what?
What's the difference between the probability you calculated from your rolls and the 1/6 you expected?
Whose data would you trust more to estimate a bent coin's chance — 20 flips or 500 flips? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: computes each experimental probability as that number's frequency ÷ 60 from the actual tally, notes the values are close to but not exactly 1/6, explains the differences as normal short-run variation, and predicts that 600 rolls would bring the relative frequencies CLOSER to 1/6 — not that each number lands exactly 100 times.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects experimental results to equal the theoretical value and concludes bias from a short run
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the mechanics — extend the run (or pool data) so the relative frequency settles nearer 1/6; a deviation over few trials is expected, bias needs many trials to judge
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the die loaded because a number came up 14 rather than 10 times in 60 rolls

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute counts 'catch up' to become exactly equal with more trials (the 'due' / gambler's fallacy of convergence)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish relative frequency (approaches 1/6) from raw counts (need NOT equalise); show a long simulation where proportions converge but counts stay unequal, and each roll remains independent
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts exactly 100 of each number in 600 rolls, or says a rarely-rolled number is 'due' to appear

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one (or vice versa)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the two meanings: experimental = from the data you collected (f ÷ n); theoretical = from the equally-likely outcomes; the task asked for the one from the rolls
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked for the experimental probability from their tally, answers 1/6 instead of computing frequency ÷ 60

responseLevels.gap: States the theoretical 1/6 regardless of the data, or expects an exact match; treats any deviation as proof of bias; no relative-frequency computed from the tally
responseLevels.full: Computes relative frequency from the data, treats deviations as short-run variation, and predicts that more trials bring the relative frequency CLOSER to theoretical without the counts becoming exactly equal or any outcome being 'due'
responseLevels.partial: Computes experimental probabilities and knows they differ from theoretical, but expects exact convergence (100 each at 600) or reads ordinary variation as bias — describes results without correctly linking convergence to sample size

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a die and have them roll it 60 times, tallying each result. Then say: 'Work out the experimental probability of each number from your results. How do they compare with what you'd expect for a fair die? And what would you expect if you rolled 600 times instead of 60?' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from THEIR data or just state 1/6, whether they treat a deviation as proof of bias, and whether they think 600 rolls would give exactly 100 each.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who computes relative frequency from their own data and expects closer-not-exact convergence from one who just recites 1/6, calls the die biased on an ordinary deviation, or expects exactly 100 of each at 600 rolls. The reasoning about MORE trials is where the law-of-large-numbers understanding shows.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Ordering Likelihoods
topic.description: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
evidence: Order four or more events from least likely to most likely and justify each placement
Compare likelihoods when outcomes are not equally likely — e.g. 'Drawing red from a bag with 7 red and 3 blue is more likely than drawing blue'
Explain why some events are closer to 'even chance' and others are closer to 'certain' or 'impossible'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a bag has 8 red counters and 2 blue ones, does {{name}} understand that picking red is much more likely than picking blue — and can they put different events in order from least to most likely?

pedagogy.summary: Ordering likelihoods asks children to compare several events and rank them least-to-most likely, including situations where outcomes are unequal (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons are solvable by simple 'more/less' reasoning; the deeper demand — comparing across different totals — requires proportional reasoning, which the research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison and begin nudging children from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes.
bestPractices: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals
Make the proportional jump visible with a two-bag comparison where the bag with MORE red counters actually has a LOWER chance of red (e.g. 3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12)
Have children physically order event cards along a least→most-likely line and defend each move
Press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds', to shift attention from absolute number to proportion
Confront the 'it's random so you can't tell' response by sampling repeatedly and tallying, so order shows up in the long run
keyRepresentations: Least-to-most-likely ordering line
Two (or more) bags of counters compared side by side, part-whole visible
Spinners with sections of different sizes
Fraction/area strips linking proportion of red to chance of red
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by absolute count of favourable outcomes ('Bag B has 6 reds, Bag A only 3, so B is better') instead of proportion
The 'difference' strategy — comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) rather than the fraction of the whole
Equiprobability bias — 'it's random, so every bag/colour is equally likely and you can't rank them'
Ranking by personal desire or by which outcome happened last, rather than by composition

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 rank several chance events from least to most likely, including unequal outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons yield to simple more/less reasoning; comparing across different totals demands proportional reasoning, which research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison, then nudge attention from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes. The signature task sets up a case where the bag with MORE red counters has a LOWER chance of red (3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12), and uses repeated sampling to let a count-based guess be publicly corrected by a long-run tally.

activities.title: Rank two bags, then test by sampling
feedback: If the child ranks Bag B higher because 'six reds beats three', run the sampling: over many draws Bag A will usually pull red more often (about three in every four draws against about one in two), and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws. Then point to all the counters in each bag, blues included, and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?' and shade three-quarters of A beside one-half of B.

If the child says 'it's random, you can't tell which is better', sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable — this separates 'random' from 'equally likely'.

When the child re-ranks Bag A to the top and justifies with the share of the whole, confirm that this share is what the growing tally gets close to: over many draws the fraction of reds moves towards the share, but it rarely matches it exactly.

On the 60-red/40-blue extension, if the child now favours Bag B because the numbers are big, compare shares directly: three-fifths is still less than three-quarters, so bigger raw counts do not by themselves make a better chance.
activities.rationale: Comparing across different totals requires proportional reasoning, and children frequently fall back on raw frequency; making the count-based ordering publicly wrong and then visible as a share targets that shift. Repeated sampling addresses the belief that a random situation cannot be ranked. An editable-bag-plus-sampler arrangement is one concrete way to let a wrong ranking be tested; a physical version with real bags, replacing each counter before the next draw, and tally marks works the same way.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.

The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
learnerActions: Look at Bag A (3 red, 1 blue) and Bag B (6 red, 6 blue), both fully visible, and rank which gives the better chance of pulling red before any draws.
State a reason for the ranking out loud.

Draw many times from each bag (e.g. 50 draws each), noting each drawn counter's colour and returning it to the bag before the next draw so the proportion stays fixed, and tally how often red comes up, comparing the two tallies.
Revise the ranking if the tally contradicts the first guess, and say why — in terms of how big a share of each bag is red, not how many reds.
Look at a shaded red-fraction strip beside each tally (three-quarters of A, one-half of B) and connect the share to the observed long-run frequency.

As an extension, suppose Bag B instead held 60 red and 40 blue: check whether these bigger numbers change the ranking (60 of 100 is three-fifths, higher than one-half but still below Bag A's three-quarters, so Bag A is still the better bet).
activities.intendedInsight: A better chance of red depends on the proportion of red in the whole bag (three-quarters beats one-half), not on the raw number of red counters — so a bag with more reds can still be the worse bet.

activities.title: Order four or more events on a least→most-likely line
feedback: If the child orders by raw count of reds, swap in a card with more reds but a smaller share and ask them to predict and then check by sampling.
If the child ranks by personal preference or by which outcome happened last, redirect to the composition: 'how many out of the whole is red here?'
Press for 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds' on every placement.
activities.rationale: Physically ordering and defending each move makes the ranking an explicit, revisable claim rather than a one-off guess, and building from same-total to different-total comparisons sequences the additive before the proportional demand. Socratic challenge ('what if I doubled the blues?') surfaces the reasoning; the proportional point may land more firmly when the child can also manipulate and sample, so pair argument with testing where possible.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Physically place four or more event cards along a 'least likely → most likely' rail (e.g. different bags or spinners with varying red fractions).
Defend each placement, and each time a card is moved, say why it should sit higher or lower.
Respond to a challenge such as 'why is that one higher? what if I doubled the blues?' by giving a reason in terms of the share of the whole, not just the number of reds.
Start with cards that share the same total (so simple more/less reasoning works) before mixing in cards with different totals.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be placed in a consistent order of likelihood by comparing the proportion of favourable outcomes; same-total cases need only more/less, but different-total cases need the share of the whole.

activities.title: Spinner prediction: does section size matter?
feedback: If the child predicts roughly equal because 'it could land on either', spin and tally: red near 15 vs blue near 5 confronts the prediction and forces attention to section size.
Use the follow-up 'could the less-likely colour still come up next spin?' to separate 'more likely in the long run' from 'certain on a single trial'.
Reserve 'even chance' for cases where the outcomes genuinely match in number, so the child does not over-apply it to unequal spinners.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test on an unequal spinner directly targets equiprobability bias by letting a prediction of 'about the same' be contradicted by the tally, while the single-trial follow-up guards against treating 'more likely' as 'certain'. The graded likelihood word-scale and the restriction of 'even chance' to matched outcomes motivate comparing by composition.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Look at a spinner where red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin.
Before spinning, predict: over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and state a reason.
Spin 20 times and tally red versus blue (expect red near 15, blue near 5).
Compare the tally to the prediction and explain what the size of each section did to the outcome.
Consider follow-ups: could the less-likely colour still come up on the very next spin? What does 'more likely' actually mean here?
activities.intendedInsight: When outcomes are not equally sized, 'it could land on either' does not make them equally likely — the size (proportion) of each section governs the long-run frequency, and a more-likely outcome can still fail on a single trial.

activities.title: The 'difference' trap: 20 red vs 18 blue
feedback: If the child says the two bags are equally good because each has 2 more reds than blues, show that 3 of 4 is three-quarters while 20 of 38 is barely above one-half: equal gaps, very different chances — this forces the comparison onto the fraction of the whole.
If the child still leans on the gap, convert each bag to 'how many out of the whole is red' and compare those shares directly.
Confirm success when the child abandons the gap and ranks by the share of red in each bag.
activities.rationale: The 'difference' strategy is a documented additive fallback; pairing two bags with an identical gap but very different proportions exposes it without relying on the child already trusting the proportional rule. This is a targeted correction to use once absolute-count errors are being addressed.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
learnerActions: Compare a bag of 20 red and 18 blue with a clearly lopsided bag of 3 red and 1 blue, and decide which gives the better chance of red. Notice that BOTH bags have the same gap: 2 more reds than blues.
Explain the reasoning, noticing whether it rests on the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) or on the share of the whole.
Work out what share of each bag is red (close to one-half for 20 of 38, three-quarters for 3 of 4) and use that to place both in order.
Check the conclusion by sampling (with each counter returned before the next draw) if a count-based or difference-based answer is given.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) can mislead: 20 red and 18 blue and 3 red and 1 blue both have a gap of 2, yet 20 of 38 is almost an even chance while 3 of 4 is three-quarters — so the fraction of the whole, not the surplus of reds, decides likelihood.

constraints: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals.

A pre-ordered likelihood line with tap-to-reveal reasons ('X out of Y, so …') is a useful worked reference, but as a fixed display it does not itself let the child test a wrong ranking or carry out the proportional correction; use it to model good ordering, not as the sole activity.

Multiple-choice or drag-to-order response formats can carry the key discriminator (e.g. 3-of-4 vs 6-of-12 with distractors 'B, it has more reds' and 'the same, it's random') and can be used during teaching as well as for checking; recognition-format responses alone do not require the child to construct and defend a ranking, so pair them with spoken or written justification.

Repeated sampling is central to confronting the 'it's random, you can't tell' response: a single draw is unpredictable, but tallying many draws reveals the long-run order. Sample with replacement (return each counter) so the stated proportions stay fixed across many draws.
Always press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds'.
Reserve 'even chance' for situations where the outcomes genuinely match in number.
When observing spinners or bags, inspect the actual drawn/spun outcomes and tallies; a short run may vary from the expected proportion, so pool more draws if a run happens to mislead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled ranking likelihoods a non-spatial task where '3D adds no leverage'; this catalog-fit judgement is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than asserted. No universal claim about any medium is made here.

The suggestion that manipulation/sampling makes the proportional insight land more firmly than argument alone is a comparative-efficacy framing not established by the cited literature; it is stated with 'may' as a design suggestion only.

The sampling activities assume drawing with replacement; with only 4 and 12 counters, the child must return each drawn counter before the next draw for many-draw tallies to reflect the fixed proportion.

Sampling 50 or 20 draws yields outcomes near the expected proportions (e.g. red near 15 of 20 for a three-quarter spinner) but will vary run to run; frame these as approximate long-run tendencies, and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws or combine results across the group.

The worked numbers are internally consistent: 3 of 4 = three-quarters > 6 of 12 = one-half, so Bag A is correctly the better chance of red; 20 of 38 for the 20-red/18-blue bag is just above one-half, consistent with 'nearly even'; and 60 of 100 = three-fifths is below three-quarters, so Bag A stays ahead in the extension.
The 'difference' trap pairs two bags with an identical gap of 2 (20/18 and 3/1) so that a reds-minus-blues strategist is genuinely misled, matching the original diagnostic intent.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided so that red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin. Ask: 'Over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and why?' Have the child state a prediction AND a reason before spinning. A child who thinks 'it could land on either, so about the same' predicts roughly equal; spinning 20 times and tallying (red near 15, blue near 5) confronts that prediction and forces attention to the size of each section.
probeDeeper: What if I now told you Bag B had 60 red and 40 blue — would that change your answer? Why?
Cover up the blue counters. Just from the reds, can you tell which bag is better? What else do you need to know?
Suppose a third bag had 20 red and 18 blue — where would it go in the order, and why?
You said one is 'more likely'. Could the less-likely bag still give a red on the very next pull? So what does 'more likely' actually mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: Bag A. Even though Bag B contains more red counters (6 versus 3), three of the four counters in Bag A are red — three-quarters — while only six of the twelve in Bag B are red — one half. Bag A has the higher proportion of red, so a better chance.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by absolute count of favourable outcomes — 'Bag B, it has more red counters (6 beats 3)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Direct attention to the whole: cover the blues and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?'; shade three-quarters of A and one-half of B side by side
errorPatterns.distractor: Bag B, because it has more red counters — 6 reds, and Bag A only has 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Bag B and reasons from the raw number of reds, ignoring how many counters there are altogether

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — 'it's the same, pulling a counter is random so you can't say which bag is better'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable, separating 'random' from 'equally likely'
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the same — pulling a counter is random, so you can't say which bag is better.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says both bags are equally good and appeals to randomness/luck rather than composition

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Difference' strategy — compares by the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) rather than the proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Offer the 20-red/18-blue counterexample: a difference of 2 but almost an even chance; force the comparison onto the fraction of the whole, not the gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reason cites the surplus of reds over blues ('A has 2 more reds than blues; B has none more'); gives the wrong answer when shown a bag like 20 red / 18 blue (gap of 2 but nearly even)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot rank beyond guessing or says 'it's random, you can't tell'; ordering ignores composition entirely
responseLevels.full: Ranks by the proportion of favourable outcomes, picks Bag A and justifies with three-quarters vs one-half, and keeps the ranking correct when totals are changed; recognises a more-likely event can still fail on a single trial
responseLevels.partial: Ranks correctly when totals are equal or by counting favourable outcomes, but picks the larger-count bag when proportion and count diverge, or reasons from the red-minus-blue difference — lists the numbers without converting to a share of the whole

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two bags of counters, both visible. Bag A: 3 red and 1 blue. Bag B: 6 red and 6 blue. Ask: 'Which bag gives you a better chance of pulling out a red — and why?' Take their answer, then ask them to explain their reason fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A proportional reasoner picks Bag A and justifies with the fraction of red in each bag; a child using absolute counts picks Bag B because it has more red counters; an equiprobability-biased child says 'the same, it's random'. The Tier-2 reason exposes which, and only the proportional reason survives when the totals are then changed.

sources.claim: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

sources.claim: The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

sources.claim: Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Experimental probability
topic.description: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
evidence: Conduct a coin-toss experiment, record results in a frequency table, and calculate relative frequencies
Compare experimental results with theoretical probability and explain discrepancies
Predict that relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rolls a die 60 times and records the results, can they compare how often each number came up with what they'd expect in theory — and explain why they might not match perfectly?

pedagogy.summary: At KS3, experimental probability is treated as relative frequency (frequency ÷ number of trials) serving as an ESTIMATE of an underlying probability — crucially, an estimate that is the ONLY route when a device is biased or its structure unknown (a drawing pin, a bent coin, a real-world event). The procedure is to record outcomes in a frequency table, compute relative frequencies, compare with theoretical values where they exist, and reason that the estimate improves as trials increase.
bestPractices: Compute relative frequency from the collected data (f ÷ n), not by restating a theoretical value
Use genuinely biased or unknown devices (drawing pin, bent coin, weighted die) so relative frequency is needed as an estimate, not just a check
Show the estimate stabilising as trials grow, by pooling data or simulation, to justify 'more trials → better estimate'
Explain discrepancies between experimental and theoretical as expected short-run variation, not error or bias
Use relative frequency × number of trials to predict expected frequencies in a new run
keyRepresentations: Frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column
Relative-frequency graph stabilising as trials increase
Experimental and theoretical values marked on the same 0-to-1 scale
Biased/unknown device whose probability can only be estimated
commonMisconceptions: Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one, even for a biased/unknown device that has no calculable value
Concluding a device is biased (or fair) from too few trials (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
Treating a small-sample relative frequency as a reliable estimate of the true probability

learn.summary: KS3 experimental probability treats relative frequency (frequency ÷ number of trials) as an ESTIMATE of an underlying probability — and the only available route when a device is biased or its structure unknown (a drawing pin, a bent coin, a weighted die, a real-world event), because its probability cannot be obtained from symmetry. Learners record outcomes in a frequency table, compute relative frequencies, compare with theoretical values where they exist, and reason that the estimate becomes more reliable as trials increase. The central insight: for a device with no symmetry-derived value, the settled relative frequency IS the best estimate, and that reliability is earned by running many trials rather than by trusting a short run.

activities.title: Drop a drawing pin and watch the estimate settle
feedback: If a learner writes P(point-up) = 1/2, point out that the pin is not symmetric, so there is nothing to calculate from symmetry; the probability must be estimated from the data — relative frequency is the only route.

If a learner declares the estimate settled after only 50 drops, show the relative frequency still shifting, extend the trials or pool data so it stabilises, and state that more trials give a more reliable estimate.

If a learner expects point-up and point-down counts to become exactly equal with more drops, distinguish relative frequency (which stabilises toward the true probability) from raw counts (which need not equalise); each drop is independent, so no result is ever 'due'.

If a learner reads the settled line (e.g. around 0.63 after many trials) and offers that as the estimate while noting that trusting the 50-drop figure would have been rash, affirm that the estimate earned its reliability from the number of trials.
activities.rationale: Experimental probability is relative frequency (frequency ÷ trials) estimated from data, and the estimate approaches the true value as trials grow — a short run such as 20 or 50 trials is not enough to rely on. A biased or unknown device removes the temptation to restate a theoretical value, so the learner must compute the estimate from their own data. Large trial counts are reached by pooling class data or by a simulator, since a single learner cannot physically drop a pin thousands of times.
sourceClaims: Experimental probability is the relative frequency (frequency of the event ÷ number of trials); it estimates the probability from data, and the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the true/theoretical value — a short run (e.g. 20 trials) is not enough to rely on.
learnerActions: Take a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) whose true point-up probability cannot be worked out from symmetry, and a frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column.
Drop the pin 50 times, recording point-up/point-down tallies, then compute relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50.
State this relative frequency as your best estimate of the probability, and note explicitly that there is no theoretical value to calculate from symmetry because the pin is not symmetric.

Reach a much larger number of trials and recompute the relative frequency: pool the whole class's physical drops (same type of pin, dropped the same way onto the same kind of surface) to get into the hundreds, and/or use a hidden-true-probability pin/coin simulator (with the same frequency table and relative-frequency line) to reach 500 then 5000 trials quickly. Note that the simulator's settled value estimates the simulator's hidden probability, not your own pin's. Watch how the value jumps around early and then tends to settle near a steady figure.
Decide how much you would trust the 50-drop figure versus the large-trials figure, and say why.

Use your best estimate for your pin (from your own or pooled class drops of the same kind of pin) × number of trials to predict roughly how many point-ups to expect in a fresh run of, say, 200 drops, recognising that the actual count will vary around that prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: When a device is biased or its structure is unknown there is no formula to reach for — you must run trials. The relative frequency you read off IS your best estimate of a probability you could not calculate from symmetry, and that estimate earns its reliability from the number of trials: a 50-drop figure is rough and jumpy, while a settled line after many hundreds or thousands of trials is much more reliable, though still an estimate.

activities.title: Fair-device check: experimental versus theoretical on one scale
feedback: If a learner calls a small gap between experimental and theoretical values an 'error', reframe it as expected short-run variation that shrinks as trials grow.

If a learner judges the coin biased from a short run, explain that short runs vary a lot and gather more tosses or pool class data; for a fair coin the relative frequency tends to settle near 0.5 as trials increase (the law of large numbers), because early results get diluted by later ones rather than corrected.
activities.rationale: Comparing experimental relative frequency with theoretical probability on a shared scale makes convergence visible and names short-run variation, countering the belief that small samples must reflect the true probability. This complements the biased-device activity by showing both the case with and without a calculable value.
sourceClaims: Belief in the representativeness of small samples leads people to expect short runs to reflect the true probability and to over-trust small-sample estimates, and recency ('due') errors reflect a failure to treat trials as independent.
learnerActions: Toss an ordinary coin (or roll a fair die), record outcomes in a frequency table, and compute the relative frequency for each outcome.
Mark both your experimental relative frequency and the theoretical probability on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Explain a small gap between them as expected short-run variation rather than a mistake or evidence that the coin is biased.
Repeat with more tosses (or pool data) and see whether the experimental value tends to settle closer to the theoretical one.
activities.intendedInsight: Where a theoretical value does exist, relative frequency can be compared with it: discrepancies in a short run are normal variation, and the experimental value tends toward the theoretical as trials increase. This frames why, for a biased device with no symmetry-derived value, the relative frequency is all you have.

activities.title: Compute and judge reliability from given tables
feedback: If a learner picks the smaller sample as equally good, remind them that a larger number of trials makes the relative frequency a more reliable estimate.
If a learner tries to state a symmetry-based value for the bent coin, point out that an asymmetric device has no value obtainable from symmetry; only the data gives an estimate.
activities.rationale: Table-based computation and reliability judgements between two given samples assess relative-frequency fluency and sample-size reasoning. On their own they do not generate the data or the convergence, so they are best used after hands-on trials rather than as a substitute.
sourceClaims: Experimental probability is the relative frequency (frequency of the event ÷ number of trials); it estimates the probability from data, and the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the true/theoretical value — a short run (e.g. 20 trials) is not enough to rely on.
learnerActions: Given a completed frequency table, fill in the relative-frequency column (each outcome's frequency ÷ total trials).
Decide, for a bent coin, which of two samples (e.g. 30 trials versus 800 trials) gives the more reliable estimate of its bias, and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why you cannot calculate the bent coin's probability from symmetry.
activities.intendedInsight: Computing relative frequency from a table and judging sample-size reliability are skills that can be practised and checked — but they sit on top of the run-and-stabilise experience, which is where the meaning of 'more trials → better estimate' actually comes from.

constraints: Use a genuinely biased or unknown device (drawing pin, bent coin, weighted die, real-world event) for the core task, so relative frequency is needed as an estimate and not merely a check against a known answer.
Compute relative frequency from the collected data (f ÷ n); do not let the learner restate a theoretical value in its place.

The learner should actually run trials and watch the estimate stabilise — the convergence experience is the point, and this run-and-record-and-predict work is the curriculum evidence. Recognition-only or table-reading tasks assess the computation but do not themselves elicit the run-and-stabilise reasoning, so they should supplement rather than replace a hands-on run.
Make clear that relative frequency stabilises toward the true probability while raw counts need not equalise; avoid implying point-up and point-down counts must become equal.

Large trial counts (500/5000) are impractical to drop by hand: reach them with a hidden-true-probability simulator or by pooling class data; a physical single-learner run realistically reaches tens to a few hundred.

A live simulator (hidden-true-probability spinner or pin sampler with a frequency table, a relative-frequency line, and large-trial controls) and a physical pin/coin both deliver the estimating behaviour; neither is uniquely required. Physical tossing adds realism, while a simulator reaches large trial counts quickly — choose by what you can run, and pool class data if a physical run cannot reach many trials.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's 'static image cannot teach this' and 'dialogue cannot generate the data' claims were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements: a fixed image cannot run trials and a conversation does not itself produce the convergence data, but these are not established comparative-efficacy findings. The '3D adds nothing' framing was likewise softened — physical tossing offers realism even though the 2D table and plot capture the estimating behaviour.

Example relative-frequency figures (0.62 jumping around at 50 drops, settling near 0.63 at 5000) are illustrative of a plausible biased pin, not measured values; actual values depend on the specific pin and conditions.

The claim that a drawing pin or bent coin has 'no calculable value' is treated as a practical KS3 simplification: a physical device has some true long-run probability that could in principle be modelled, but it cannot be obtained from symmetry and so must be estimated from data. Learner-facing wording was aligned to 'cannot be calculated from symmetry' rather than an unqualified 'no value exists'.

Activity 1's large trial counts were rescoped: a single-learner physical pin-drop cannot realistically reach 5000 drops, so the step routes 500/5000 trials through a simulator or pooled class data while keeping the stabilisation insight.

probeDeeper: Why can't you just calculate this probability the way you would for a fair die?
Your estimate after 50 drops is 0.6 — how much would you trust it? What would make you trust it more?
If you dropped it 5000 times, what would happen to the relative frequency? Would the counts of up and down become equal?
Two students estimate the pin: one from 30 drops, one from 800. Whose estimate would you use, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: records point-up/point-down in the table, computes relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50, and offers THAT as the best estimate — recognising there is no theoretical value to calculate because the pin is not symmetric — while noting that 50 drops gives only a rough estimate and more trials would make it more reliable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports a theoretical value for a device that has none (says P(point-up) = 1/2 for a drawing pin)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the pin is not symmetric, so there is nothing to calculate; the probability must be estimated from the data — relative frequency is the only route
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 1/2 (or another symmetry-based value) instead of computing relative frequency from the drops

errorPatterns.pattern: Concludes the probability confidently from too few trials (law of small numbers)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the relative frequency still shifting; extend trials or pool data so the estimate stabilises, and state that more trials give a more reliable estimate
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Declares the estimate settled after 50 drops with no caveat, or would judge fairness from a short run

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish relative frequency (stabilises toward the true probability) from raw counts (need not equalise); each drop is independent
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects point-up and point-down counts to become equal, or says a result is 'due'

responseLevels.gap: States a theoretical value the device does not have, or treats a short-run relative frequency as exact; no sense that the estimate depends on trials
responseLevels.full: Estimates the probability by relative frequency from the data, recognises no theoretical value exists for the pin, treats 50 drops as limited, and states that more trials make the estimate more reliable as relative frequency stabilises
responseLevels.partial: Computes relative frequency from the data and knows it estimates the probability, but trusts a small sample without caveat, or expects counts to equalise — reports a number without reasoning about reliability

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) and a frequency table. Say: 'Find the probability that this pin lands point-up. Drop it 50 times, record the results, and tell me your best estimate of the probability — and whether 50 drops is enough.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from their data or try to state a theoretical 1/2, how they treat the variation, and whether they judge 50 drops as limited.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who estimates from their own data and hedges on 50 trials from one who states '1/2' (a theoretical value the pin does not have), treats the count as exact, or trusts 50 drops as definitive. Because the pin has no calculable probability, defaulting to theory is exposed immediately.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Probability models
topic.description: Develop a probability model (a list of all the outcomes of a chance process with a probability for each, adding to 1) and use it to find probabilities of events: a uniform model gives every outcome the same probability (e.g. selecting a student at random from a class); a non-uniform model uses probabilities estimated from the observed frequencies of a chance process (e.g. how a tossed paper cup lands); compare a model's probabilities with observed frequencies and, when they disagree, explain whether the difference is plausibly chance variation or a sign that the model does not fit (e.g. a biased die or unequal spinner sections)
evidence: Use a uniform model to find that a randomly chosen student from a class of 25 with 12 girls is Jane with probability 1/25 and is a girl with probability 12/25
Toss a paper cup 50 times (e.g. 31 on its side, 13 open end up, 6 open end down), write a model with probabilities 0.62, 0.26 and 0.12, and explain why the three outcomes are not equally likely
Compare 600 rolls of a die that showed 160 sixes with the 100 sixes a fair-die model predicts, and argue that a difference this large suggests the die is biased rather than just chance
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a paper cup 50 times and records whether it lands on its side, open end up or open end down, could they turn the results into a probability for each way of landing — and say whether the three are equally likely?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Simulating chance events
topic.description: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated and when the trial stops) and the event being counted; run many trials; and estimate the probability as the event's relative frequency. Explain why the model fits (each simulated outcome has the same probability as the real one, and successive outcomes are independent when the real ones are), and why different runs give different estimates that become more consistent as the number of trials grows; where a theoretical value can be found (e.g. with a tree diagram), compare it with the estimate
evidence: Map random digits 0–3 to 'type A' and 4–9 to 'not type A' to model donors who are type A with probability 40%, and explain why the mapping fits (4 of the 10 equally likely digits)

Define one trial as reading digits until the first 0–3 appears, count it as a success if at least four digits were needed, run 50 trials and report the relative frequency as the estimated probability that at least four donors are needed
Explain why two groups who each ran 50 trials estimated 0.18 and 0.26, and why pooling their trials (or running 500) gives a more reliable estimate
topic.assessmentPrompt: If 40% of blood donors are type A, could {{name}} use random numbers or a spinner to act out lots of donor queues, estimate how often at least four donors are needed before the first type A — and explain why doing it again gives a slightly different answer?

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Probability as a Fraction
topic.description: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
evidence: State that the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 and explain why
Express the probability of picking a red card from a standard deck as 26/52 or 1/2
Write the probability of a simple event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a fair coin, do they know the probability of getting heads is 1/2 — and can they express similar simple probabilities as fractions and place them on a 0-to-1 scale?

pedagogy.summary: Probability as a fraction is the child's first symbolic representation of chance: for equally-likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes (P(6) = 1/6, P(heads) = 1/2). The teaching work is translating fluently between a situation, its probability fraction, and a position on the 0-to-1 scale, while holding onto the part-WHOLE meaning (favourable out of the total) rather than the more intuitive part-part ratio.
bestPractices: Derive the fraction from the equally-likely outcomes the child can see and count — six faces, one favourable → 1/6 — not as a rule to memorise

Insist on part-whole: the denominator is the TOTAL number of equally likely outcomes, the numerator the favourable ones; contrast explicitly with odds/ratio (1 red to 5 others is written 1/6, not 1/5)
Immediately place each fraction on the 0-to-1 scale so the symbol gains a magnitude (1/6 near 0, 1/2 at the middle)
Use reducible cases (26/52 = 1/2) to connect counting outcomes with equivalent fractions
Stress that favourable/total gives the probability only when outcomes are equally likely
keyRepresentations: favourable/total fraction written under the situation
0-to-1 probability scale with the fraction marked
Dice, coins, and bags with countable equally-likely outcomes
Area/part-whole diagrams linking the fraction to the whole set of outcomes
commonMisconceptions: Writing the probability as a part-part ratio/odds (1/5 or 1:5 for one red among six) instead of the part-whole fraction 1/6
Answering with a raw frequency or whole number ('3', or Fischbein & Gazit's '3/4 and 4/3') rather than favourable-over-total
Swapping numerator and denominator — putting the total on top
Applying favourable/total to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year-olds write the probability of an equally-likely event as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (P(6)=1/6, P(heads)=1/2, one of three equally represented colours = 1/3), and translate fluently between a situation, its fraction, and a point on the 0-to-1 scale. The central work is holding the part-WHOLE meaning (favourable out of the TOTAL) against the more intuitive part-part ratio/odds, and attaching the symbol to a magnitude on the scale.

activities.title: Build the fraction from a bag, and place it on the 0-to-1 line
feedback: If a child writes 1/5 for one red among six: recount the whole set aloud including the red — the bottom number is every counter that could be drawn (6), not just the others (5).
If a child swaps to 6/1 or puts the total on top: a probability is never bigger than 1, so the whole (total) sits on the bottom and the favourable part on top.
When the counters change and both the fraction and marker move, name it: 'The symbol and its position on the scale moved together.'
activities.rationale: The topic is translation across three linked representations (situation ↔ fraction ↔ point on the scale). An editable bag whose fraction recomputes and whose marker slides makes the translation visible and reversible, and deriving the fraction from countable equally-likely outcomes keeps it meaningful rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.

Children reason more naturally with part-part ratios than part-whole fractions, and a documented additive error (Fischbein & Gazit) is giving the frequencies of outcomes as the probability (answering '3/4 and 4/3'), rather than favourable-over-total.
learnerActions: Fill a bag with coloured counters that are identical apart from colour, which you can see and count, and that will be drawn without looking — e.g. drop in one red among six total.
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction: count the favourable (reds) for the numerator and the WHOLE set (all counters, red included) for the denominator, giving 1/6.
Mark that fraction on a 0-to-1 line (1/6 hugging 0, 1/2 at the middle).
Add more reds and re-count: watch the fraction change and the marker slide up the line together.
Deliberately test the wrong answer: try to make it 1/5 (red to the other five) and re-count the total to see the denominator counts all six counters, not the leftovers.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the total number of equally likely outcomes (every counter that could be drawn), not the count of the OTHER outcomes; the fraction has a size you can locate between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Interpret a given fraction: what does each number count?
feedback: If the child says 6 is 'the other faces' or 'the ones that aren't 6': the 6 counts every face, including the favourable one.
Prompt: 'In 1/6, why is 6 on the bottom and not 5? What is the 6 counting?'
Prompt: 'Could this fraction ever be bigger than 1? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Interpreting a prepared fraction cleanly separates reading the symbol from constructing it, and tap-to-reveal makes the part-whole structure explicit. This is a scaffold for the interpret half; on its own it does not require the child to construct a fraction from a new situation.
sourceClaims: Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.
learnerActions: Look at a fair six-sided die alongside the statement P(rolling a 6) = 1/6.
Say what the 1 stands for (one favourable face) and what the 6 stands for (the total number of equally likely faces).
On a labelled die or bag, tap the favourable outcomes to reveal the numerator, then tap the whole set to reveal the denominator.
Then reveal where that fraction sits on the 0-to-1 scale.
activities.intendedInsight: In favourable/total, the numerator counts the outcomes you want and the denominator counts ALL equally likely outcomes; the fraction names a magnitude on the scale.

activities.title: Construct and translate from a fresh situation
feedback: If the child writes 3/2 or 3:2: recount the whole set aloud including the reds — the denominator is every counter that could be drawn (5), so the total goes on the bottom, not the leftovers (2).
If the child answers with a raw count ('3'): a probability is always a part of the whole, written as a fraction (or decimal/percent) between 0 and 1, never a plain count.
P(red) and P(not red) together should make 1 (whole bag); use this to check the fraction (here 3/5 and 2/5).
For 26/52: counting 26 favourable of 52 total gives the same value as 1/2 — the equivalent fraction.
activities.rationale: Constructing favourable/total from a fresh situation exercises the translation the topic requires and surfaces the part-part misconception documented in the literature; reducible and simple fair cases link outcome-counting to equivalent fractions.
sourceClaims: Children reason more naturally with part-part ratios than part-whole fractions, and a documented additive error (Fischbein & Gazit) is giving the frequencies of outcomes as the probability (answering '3/4 and 4/3'), rather than favourable-over-total.
Probability of an equally-likely event is written as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (e.g. P(red)=1/6), expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage — not as an integer.
learnerActions: Take a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter (5 in total).
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, forming favourable-over-total: 3/5.
Mark 3/5 on a 0-to-1 scale (a little above the halfway point).
Then write the probability of NOT red and check what the two fractions add up to.
Try another fair case: a bag with three equally represented colours gives P(one colour) = 1/3, marked a little below the halfway point on the scale.
Reduce a case where it applies: a standard 52-card deck has 26 red cards, so P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2 — connect counting outcomes to equivalent fractions.
activities.intendedInsight: Building the fraction from a NEW situation — not reading a prepared one — is where part-whole understanding shows: a part-whole reasoner writes 3/5, a part-part reasoner writes 3/2 or 3:2 (red to non-red).

activities.title: Check the outcomes are equally likely before counting
feedback: If a child writes a simple fraction for an uneven spinner as if the regions were equal: check first that outcomes are equally likely; if they aren't, the colour counts are not the counts of equally likely outcomes, so favourable/total does not apply directly.
activities.rationale: Best practice stresses that favourable/total is valid only for equally-likely outcomes; making this check explicit guards against misapplying the rule.
learnerActions: Before writing favourable/total, ask: are all the outcomes equally likely?
Compare a fair die or a bag of identical counters (equally likely) with an uneven spinner whose regions differ in size (not equally likely).
For the uneven case, notice why counting colours or regions does not directly give the probability.
activities.intendedInsight: favourable/total gives the probability only when the outcomes are equally likely; otherwise the counts of colours/regions are not counts of equally likely outcomes.

activities.title: Talk it through: why that number on the bottom?
feedback: Catch a part-part answer and ask the child to recount the whole set.

For the 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag: if they say adding two greens doesn't change anything, the total (denominator) grows from 5 to 7 while the reds (numerator) stay at 3, so the probability of red falls from 3/5 to 3/7.
activities.rationale: Socratic prompts surface part-whole reasoning and misconceptions in the child's own words. Discussion supports the symbol work but linking symbol to magnitude is better shown on a scale than only talked about.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'What goes on the bottom of the fraction, and why?'
If you give a part-part answer, re-count the whole set and explain which outcomes the denominator includes.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Calculating Simple Probability
topic.description: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
evidence: Calculate the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag of 3 blue and 7 red as 3/10
Use the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes to solve at least three different problems
Explain why increasing the number of favourable outcomes increases the probability
topic.assessmentPrompt: If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, can {{name}} work out the probability of picking a red one and express it as a fraction in its simplest form?

pedagogy.summary: Calculating simple probability is the procedural skill of applying P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes to equally-likely situations and giving the answer as a fraction in simplest form. The work is fluent, accurate execution across contexts (dice, bags, spinners): counting the favourable outcomes, counting the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), forming the fraction, checking the outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying.
bestPractices: Rehearse the same three-step routine across varied contexts — count favourable, count total, write and simplify — so it transfers beyond dice
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes (favourable included), heading off the part-part error
Require a check that outcomes are equally likely BEFORE applying the formula
Connect 'more favourable outcomes → larger probability' by varying a bag's composition and watching the fraction grow
Always express in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale
keyRepresentations: P(event) = favourable/total written under the situation
Bags, dice, spinners with countable equally-likely outcomes
Simplified-fraction equivalence (2/8 = 1/4) on the 0-to-1 scale
Part-whole diagram of the outcome set

Failing to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly

learn.summary: Learners build fluency with P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally-likely situations, giving answers as fractions in simplest form. The core routine is: check the outcomes are equally likely, count favourable outcomes, count the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), form the fraction, and simplify. Practice should span varied contexts (dice, bags, spinners) and target the part-part error (favourable-to-unfavourable) and the misapplication of the formula to unequal outcomes.

activities.title: Varied probability ladder with simplest form
feedback: If a learner writes 3/7 for the bag, recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes: everything that could be drawn is 10, so 10 goes on the bottom, giving 3/10.

If a learner applies the formula to an uneven spinner, prompt the equally-likely check first: when sections are different sizes the colour counts are not counts of equally-likely outcomes, so the simple formula does not apply.

If a learner leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly, scaffold the simplifying step and confirm 1/4 sits at the same point on the 0-to-1 scale \u2014 simplifying does not change the actual chance.
If a learner combines numbers arbitrarily with no favourable-over-total structure, return to counting favourable, then total, then writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: The objective is fluent, accurate execution of favourable/total across contexts with simplest-form answers. Varied contexts support transfer beyond dice, and items built from the exact errors (part-part, unsimplified, formula on an uneven spinner) make the common mistakes surface and get corrected.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.

learnerActions: Work a short series of problems, each a probability to be formed and then simplified: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles \u2014 find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die \u2014 find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold \u2014 find P(gold).
For each item, first confirm the outcomes are equally likely, then count the favourable outcomes, then count the WHOLE set of possible outcomes (including the favourable ones) for the denominator.
Write each probability as a fraction and simplify where possible (e.g. 2/8 \u2192 1/4).
On the bag item, if you write 3/7, stop and recount: the denominator is all 10 marbles, including the 3 blue ones, so the answer is 3/10.
Encounter at least one unequal-outcome situation (e.g. an uneven spinner with different-sized sections) and decide whether the simple formula applies before using it.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the whole set of equally-likely outcomes, favourable included \u2014 so P(blue) among 3 blue and 7 red is 3/10, not 3/7. The simple favourable/total formula only applies when outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying (2/8 = 1/4) names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.

activities.title: Editable bag: watch the fraction form and simplify
feedback: If a learner expects only the numerator to matter, vary the non-favourable counts and show that the denominator (whole set) and the scale marker both respond \u2014 e.g. adding red marbles enlarges the total, so P(blue) falls (as long as the bag has at least one blue; with no blue it stays 0).
Confirm that the simplified fraction lands on the same point of the 0-to-1 line as the unsimplified one \u2014 the chance is unchanged.

This may support conceptual understanding alongside the procedural fluency. The interactive updating (live fraction, scale marker) is an optional illustrative mechanism, not required equipment.

learnerActions: Edit the composition of a bag (e.g. add or remove blue and red counters) and read the probability fraction as it forms.
Identify the WHOLE set as the denominator each time the bag changes, confirming favourable counters are part of that total.
Watch the simplified form of the fraction and a marker on a 0-to-1 line move as the composition changes.
Predict: 'If I add 5 more red marbles, which number in the fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?' then check against the live display.

When asked 'and out of how many altogether?', state the full count of possible outcomes, not just the non-favourable ones.
