topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Probabilities Sum to One
topic.description: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
evidence: List all outcomes of spinning a 4-colour spinner and verify their probabilities add up to 1
Calculate P(not rolling a 3) as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 using the complement rule
Spot an error in a probability table where the values don't sum to 1 and explain what's wrong
topic.assessmentPrompt: If the probability of it raining tomorrow is 0.3, can {{name}} work out the probability of it NOT raining — and explain why all probabilities in a situation must add up to 1?

pedagogy.summary: Probabilities sum to one captures a structural truth: when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial, their probabilities must total 1. This lets a child find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) rather than counting every unfavourable outcome. The concept rests on the outcomes being both mutually exclusive and exhaustive — covering the whole of what can happen, with no overlap.
bestPractices: Model the whole of possibility as a bar of length 1 partitioned among the outcomes, so 'the rest of the bar' IS the complement
Establish that the list must be exhaustive (covers everything) and mutually exclusive (no overlaps) before the sum-to-1 argument applies
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as a shortcut, contrasting it with the slower count-all-the-others method on the same problem
Use spot-the-error tables whose probabilities don't total 1, and ask what must be wrong
Link back to calculating simple probabilities so children see favourable + unfavourable together exhaust the outcomes
keyRepresentations: Unit bar (length 1) partitioned into outcome segments
Complete outcome table with probabilities totalling 1
P(not A) shown as the remaining part of the whole
Spinner whose sectors fill the entire disc
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring the sum-to-1 constraint and assigning a missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy to another
Treating 'not A' as a single other outcome rather than everything except A, or thinking P(not A) equals P(A)
Adding probabilities of overlapping or non-exhaustive events and still expecting them to total 1
Adding fractions without a common denominator when totalling probabilities

learn.summary: Teach that when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial — with no overlaps and nothing left out — their probabilities must total exactly 1. This lets a learner find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) instead of counting every unfavourable outcome. The reasoning only holds when the outcomes are mutually exclusive (no overlap) and exhaustive (cover everything).

activities.title: Fill the unit bar: the leftover IS the missing probability
feedback: If the learner says green = 1/6 'like blue': add the given segments (1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3) and point to the strip still unfilled — the missing value is whatever completes the whole to 1, not a copy of another outcome.
If segments overshoot the bar or leave a gap: these probabilities don't total 1, so the list is impossible — check it covers everything with no overlap.
If 'not red' is named as just blue or just green: highlight the whole rest of the bar — 'not red' means every outcome except red (blue AND green together).
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit whole makes both sum-to-1 and the complement concrete: the remaining segment is literally the missing or complementary value, and an over- or under-filled bar flags an impossible set. This directly targets the misconception of assigning an 'equal' value by analogy.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Take a bar exactly one unit long that stands for everything that can happen when you draw a counter from a bag of red, blue and green counters.
Set red to one-half of the bar and blue to one-sixth, marking those segments.
Before being told, work out what must fill the remaining strip and state it: green = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3.
Mark 'P(not red)' by highlighting the entire rest of the bar (blue and green together) and give its value as 1 − P(red) = 1/2.
State in words why green could NOT be a free choice and why 'green must be 1/6 like blue' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole of possibility has length 1; once some outcomes are placed, the leftover segment IS the missing probability, and 'not red' is the whole rest of the bar — everything except red — not a single other colour.

activities.title: Spinner that fills the whole disc
feedback: If the prediction ignores the total (e.g. guesses arbitrarily or copies a colour): add the known sectors and show how much of the disc is still empty — that gap is the missing probability.
If the fraction sum is slipped: rewrite with a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, so together 5/6; the rest is 1/6) before subtracting from 1.
activities.rationale: A full disc reinforces exhaustiveness visually and gives a second representation of the same structural truth, supporting learners who grasp area more readily than a linear bar; representing the full set of outcomes directly addresses the sample-space misconception.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Look at (or draw) a spinner whose coloured sectors must fill the entire disc with no gap and no overlap.
Given red = one-half and blue = one-third, predict the remaining sector's probability (yellow) before it is revealed: 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6.
Check the revealed sector really is a sixth of the disc.
Tap or mark each sector in turn and track the running total as it reaches exactly 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A spinner's sectors are another model of the whole-equals-1 idea: because the sectors must fill the disc, the last sector's size (and probability) is forced by the others.

activities.title: Complement shortcut versus counting the others
feedback: If the learner thinks P(not A) equals P(A): contrast the two methods — 'not 3' on a die is five outcomes out of six (5/6), clearly not the same as P(3) = 1/6.
If 'not A' is treated as a single other outcome: list what 'not A' actually contains and show it is every outcome except A.
If the learner struggles with the compound case: note that 'red or blue' already covers two of the three exhaustive colours, so green is simply whatever is left of the whole — 1 − 3/4 = 1/4.
activities.rationale: Running the slow count-all-the-others method alongside the subtraction shortcut on the same problem makes the equivalence explicit and justifies why the shortcut works, rather than presenting it as a rule to memorise.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Calculate P(not rolling a 3) on a fair six-sided die two ways: first by subtracting, 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; then by counting all the other outcomes (1,2,4,5,6) and adding their probabilities (five sixths).
Compare the two methods, note they give the same answer, and that subtracting from 1 is faster when there are many unfavourable outcomes.
For the counter bag, find P(not red) as 1 − P(red) = 1/2 and confirm it matches blue + green (1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2).

Extend to a compound complement: a different bag of red, blue and green counters has P(red or blue) = 3/4; find P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, since each counter is exactly one of the three colours and the three colours exhaust the bag.
activities.intendedInsight: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is a shortcut for 'everything except A', and it equals the sum of all the other outcomes because together they fill the whole; the same subtraction works when the known part is a compound event like 'red or blue'.

activities.title: Spot the impossible table
feedback: If a learner accepts 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6: show the sum is 5/6, not 1, so one value must change — there is no rule forcing green to match blue.
If the learner cannot add the fractions: use a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6) before totalling, giving 3/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
activities.rationale: Error-spotting forces the learner to apply the constraint actively rather than restate it, and directly confronts the equiprobability-by-analogy misconception.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Examine probability tables and decide which are impossible because the values do not total 1 (e.g. a table listing 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6 for three colours).
Add the values, compare the total with 1, and explain exactly what is wrong.
Correct one impossible table by finding the value that would make it total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A complete list of outcomes that does not total 1 cannot be right. Checking the sum is a necessary test, but it is not enough on its own: a valid probability distribution also needs every value to be between 0 and 1, and the outcomes must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

activities.title: When the sum-to-1 argument does NOT apply: overlapping events
feedback: If a learner adds overlapping events' probabilities and is satisfied the total is 1: show that P(even or prime) is really 5/6, because outcome 2 was counted in both 'even' and 'prime' — reaching 1 here is a coincidence, not a valid use of sum-to-1.
If a learner thinks the rule never applies to dice: clarify it does apply to a complete list of distinct single outcomes (1–6), just not to overlapping compound events.
activities.rationale: Making the conditions explicit prevents over-generalising the rule. 'Even' and 'prime' sharing 2 on a die is a documented student error, so naming the overlap condition — and showing that its naive sum equals 1 by coincidence while the true union is 5/6 — guards against it.

Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Consider rolling a fair die and the events 'even' and 'prime'. List the outcomes for each: even = {2,4,6}, prime = {2,3,5}.
Notice that 2 belongs to both, so the events overlap and are NOT mutually exclusive.

Add P(even) = 3/6 and P(prime) = 3/6 and notice the total comes to 1 — then find the true chance of 'even or prime': the combined outcomes are {2,3,4,5,6}, which is 5/6, not 1. The naive sum reached 1 only by counting outcome 2 twice.
Explain why adding probabilities of overlapping events double-counts the shared outcome, so the total does not give P(even or prime), even when the arithmetic happens to land on 1.
Contrast with the counter-bag colours, which are mutually exclusive (a counter is exactly one colour) and exhaustive, so there the probabilities genuinely total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Sum-to-1 and the complement shortcut only hold when the listed events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; with overlapping events, adding probabilities double-counts shared outcomes, and the total — even if it coincidentally equals 1 — does not represent the combined event.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: do your outcomes cover everything?
feedback: If the learner cannot justify the total: return to the bar or disc model where the whole visibly equals 1.
If the learner asserts equal likelihood by habit: ask what evidence fixes each value — the total constraint, not similarity to another colour.
activities.rationale: Prompting for the conditions and the justification surfaces whether the learner is actually using the constraint and targets the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely; this works best alongside a filled-whole representation rather than in isolation.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Respond to prompts such as 'Do your outcomes cover everything, with no overlap?' and 'What do they add up to?'
Defend or revise a claim like 'so green must be 1/6 too' by appealing to the sum-to-1 constraint.
Explain in your own words why all the outcomes must add to exactly 1 — not more and not less.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the exhaustive-and-mutually-exclusive conditions and the total-equals-1 constraint strengthens reasoning beyond pattern-matching.

constraints: The sum-to-1 argument and P(not A) = 1 − P(A) require the listed outcomes to be mutually exclusive (no overlap) AND exhaustive (cover everything); establish both conditions before applying the rule.
Do not present 'each outcome is equally likely' as a default; the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness between outcomes, fixes a missing value.

Adding probabilities of overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die) double-counts shared outcomes; the resulting total does not represent the combined event even when it coincidentally equals 1 (here P(even)+P(prime)=1 but the true P(even or prime)=5/6). This is a condition failure, not a sum-to-1 counterexample.
Totalling probabilities given as fractions requires a common denominator; a wrong total here is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception, and should be scaffolded separately.

A static tap-to-reveal partitioned bar or disc can show a complete set totalling 1 but does not let the learner test an incomplete or overlapping list; use it as a display scaffold, then move to a task where the learner constructs or corrects a list.

Choosing the impossible table from options can check whether a learner applies the constraint but does not by itself show the learner can independently construct a valid distribution; pair it with a construction task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit: every fraction sum and outcome set was re-derived — green = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3; spinner yellow = 1 − 5/6 = 1/6; P(not 3) = 5/6 (matches counting 1,2,4,5,6); impossible table 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6 ≠ 1; compound complement P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4; overlap P(even)+P(prime) = 3/6 + 3/6 = 1 while the true union {2,3,4,5,6} = 5/6. All consistent, and the overlap activity makes the coincidence explicit rather than claiming the sum fails to reach 1.

The legacy entry rated a 3D interactive 'poor' on the basis that '3D adds nothing'; this ranking is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than restated as a universal claim. Sum-to-1 is well modelled in 1D/2D, but no claim is made that a 3D medium could add nothing.

The legacy 'possible' static-image and conversation formats are preserved as the tap-to-reveal scaffold and the Socratic activity respectively, with their narrow observable limits placed in constraints rather than asserted as 'cannot teach' claims.
The tempting wrong answer '1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue' is retained only as a misconception to confront in feedback, never offered as a correct option.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided into unequal sectors you have pre-measured: red is one-half, blue is one-third, yellow is one-sixth. Cover the yellow sector. Say: 'The red part is a half and the blue is a third. Before I uncover the last colour, predict the probability of yellow — and explain how you got it.' A child ignoring sum-to-1 guesses arbitrarily or says 'a third, like blue'; the sum-to-1 reasoner predicts 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6. Uncover the sector and check it really is a sixth of the disc. The reason given BEFORE uncovering is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What is P(not red) for this bag? How did you get it — by adding colours or by taking red from the whole?
If I told you the three probabilities were 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6, what would be wrong with that?
Why do all the outcomes have to add up to exactly 1, and not more or less?
Suppose a bag had red, blue and green but you were told P(red or blue) = 3/4 — what is P(green)?
assess.correctAnswer: P(green) = 1/3. All the outcomes must total 1, so P(green) = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. The classmate is wrong: there is no rule that each colour is equally likely — the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness with blue, fixes the missing value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sum-to-1 constraint and assigns the missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy ('green is 1/6, the same as blue')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the given probabilities and show they don't yet reach 1; the missing value is whatever completes the whole, so subtract from 1 rather than copy another outcome
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(green) = 1/6 or reasons that the colours must be equally likely, without checking the total

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'not A' as a single other outcome, or thinks P(not A) equals P(A), rather than everything except A
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show P(not red) as the whole rest of the bar (blue and green together) = 1 − P(red); 'not red' is every outcome except red, not a single one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up 'what is P(not red)?' names just one colour, or gives 1/2 as if 'not red' mirrors red

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the fractions without a common denominator when totalling
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the common-denominator step (1/2 = 3/6, so 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6); this is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 1/2 + 1/6 as 2/8 or similar, then subtracts wrongly

responseLevels.gap: Assigns the missing probability with no regard to the total; cannot find P(not A) except by trying to list every other outcome, often wrongly
responseLevels.full: Uses sum-to-1 to find the missing probability (1/3) and P(not A) = 1 − P(A), justifies by the outcomes being exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and spots tables that cannot be right because they don't total 1
responseLevels.partial: Knows outcomes should total 1 and can find a missing value in the simplest cases, but copies another outcome's value, mishandles 'not A', or slips on the fraction arithmetic — states the rule without applying it reliably

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bag holds red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 1/2 and P(blue) = 1/6. A classmate says P(green) must be 1/6 as well, 'because green is just one colour, the same as blue'. Ask the child: is the classmate right? What is P(green), and why? Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reasoning fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sum-to-1 reasoner subtracts the known probabilities from 1; the surface reasoner copies blue's value or assumes the colours are equal; a complement-confused child mishandles what 'the rest' means. The Tier-2 explanation reveals whether the total-equals-1 constraint was actually used.

sources.claim: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: The 0-to-1 Probability Scale
topic.description: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
evidence: Place events on a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressing positions as fractions or decimals
Explain that a probability of 0.5 means 'even chance' and connect this to the informal word 'likely'
Convert between informal language ('very unlikely') and a numerical position on the 0-to-1 scale
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal, and a percentage — for example, knowing that an even chance is ½, 0.5, and 50%?

pedagogy.summary: The 0-to-1 probability scale formalises chance as a measured quantity: every probability is a number from 0 (impossible) through 1/2 (even chance) to 1 (certain), and can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage. The teaching aim is to treat probability as a magnitude on a bounded number line — placing events, converting freely between the three notations, and connecting 0.5 back to the informal 'even chance'.
bestPractices: Anchor a single 0-to-1 line marked with the landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance), 1 (certain) and use it as the home for every probability
Show the SAME point written three ways — 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% — so children see the notations as one magnitude, not three separate things
Move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood
Stress the bounds: nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1), so a probability can never be negative or exceed 1
Reconnect 0.5 to 'even chance' and small values to 'unlikely', linking the numeric scale to the words learned earlier
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line with 0, 1/2, 1 landmarks (impossible / even / certain)
Triple-notation labels (fraction = decimal = percentage) at each position
Event cards placed along the line
Links from likelihood words to numeric positions
commonMisconceptions: Believing a probability can be greater than 1, or giving a probability as a raw count (e.g. '6' because a die has six outcomes)
Fraction interference — thinking a larger denominator means a larger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
Comparing mixed notations by surface digits without converting (ranking 40%, 1/4, 0.3 as 40 > 4 > 0.3)
Treating 0.5 / 'even chance' as the default for any two-outcome event

learn.summary: Teach probability as a magnitude on a bounded 0-to-1 line, with landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain). The same probability can be written three ways — fraction, decimal and percentage (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) — and children should move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood. Stress the bounds (never below 0 or above 1) and reconnect 0.5 to the informal 'even chance' learned earlier. Comparing mixed notations requires converting to a common form, not ranking by surface digits or by denominator size.

activities.title: One position, three notations on a draggable scale
feedback: When the three notations appear together at one point, point out: these are not three different chances but one position written three ways.
If the learner expects '2' to be placeable, note that the scale stops at 1 because nothing is more likely than certain — a probability can never be a raw count like 6.
Blocking the drag past 0 and 1 makes the bounds felt directly; name them as impossible and certain as the marker reaches each end.
activities.rationale: Showing the same point as fraction, decimal and percentage at once targets the core idea that these notations are one magnitude. Blocking movement past the endpoints makes the bounds concrete and confronts the belief that a probability can exceed 1 or be a count. The live three-way readout and snap-to-line examples are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Drag a marker along a 0-to-1 line; a readout shows wherever you land simultaneously as a fraction, a decimal AND a percentage, so 2/5, 0.4 and 40% appear together at the same point.
Place the 'chance of rain 40%' event and watch the marker coincide exactly with 0.4 and 2/5 — confirm these are one position written three ways, not three different chances.
Feed a computed probability from a bag or spinner and watch it snap onto the line at its matching position.
Try to shove the marker past the 'certain' end for a 'probability of 2' and notice it refuses to move beyond 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is a single magnitude on a bounded line; the fraction, decimal and percentage are three ways of writing the same position, and nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1).

activities.title: Place, order and match mixed-notation probabilities
feedback: If a learner ranks 40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by surface digits, convert all three to decimals (0.4, 0.25, 0.3) or mark them on the line; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3.

If a learner treats 1/4 as largest because of the 4 in the denominator, return to meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one part out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare.

For a value above 1 or below 0, re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0). When outcomes are equally likely, probability is favourable-over-total; the favourable count can never exceed the total or be negative, so the probability is at most 1 and never below 0.
activities.rationale: Placement, ordering and matching tasks rehearse exactly the conversions and placements the topic demands. Requiring conversion to a common form targets the documented tendency to fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons. The ordering answer 1/4=0.25, 0.3, 0.4 was checked: 0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4 is correct.
sourceClaims: Quantifying and comparing probabilities requires proportional reasoning; children commonly fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons rather than converting to a common proportion, a persistent difficulty documented across the probability literature.
learnerActions: Use a slider to place 1/4 and 0.7 on the 0-to-1 line.
Order 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely, converting each to a common form (decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4) before deciding.
Match equivalent forms: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.
Spot and reject an impossible probability, such as a value greater than 1 or below 0, explaining why it cannot be a valid probability.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing probabilities written in different notations requires converting to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line); surface digits and denominator size are not reliable guides, and every valid probability lies between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Landmark reference line with revealed equivalents
feedback: Confirm that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% all mark the even-chance midpoint, linking back to the informal word learned earlier.
Prompt the learner to supply their own event for 0 and for 1 to check they grasp impossible and certain.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference line with tap-to-reveal equivalents clearly presents the triple notation and links words to positions. As a reference it does not let the child test a mis-placement, so it supports but does not replace active placement work; this limit is recorded in constraints.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Tap each landmark (0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1) to reveal its fraction, decimal and percentage.
At each landmark, read an everyday event that belongs there (e.g. an impossible event at 0, a certain event at 1, an even-chance event at 1/2).
Use the revealed values as a reference while completing placement and ordering tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each landmark on the scale has a fixed fraction/decimal/percentage identity and a matching kind of everyday event, giving a stable reference for the triple notation.

activities.title: Socratic probing of the bounds
feedback: When the learner says a value cannot be placed, name the reason: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0).

Redirect a count answer ('6 because a die has six outcomes') to favourable-over-total for a fair die's equally likely outcomes: the number of favourable outcomes can never be more than the total, so the fraction is never more than 1 (for example, 6/6 = 1 means certain).

If the learner assumes every two-outcome event is an even chance, point out that 0.5 applies only when the two outcomes are equally likely; many two-outcome events (e.g. a biased spinner) are not 1/2.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge surfaces the greater-than-1, count, and even-chance-default misconceptions by asking the child to justify and locate claimed values and to test a tempting generalisation. Discussion raises the ideas, but placing magnitudes may be clearer when also shown on a line, so pair this with the draggable or reference activities rather than using it alone.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'the probability is 6' or 'could a probability be 2?' by explaining what 0 and 1 mean.
Locate a claimed value like '6' or '2' on the 0-to-1 line and explain why it cannot sit there.
Describe an event at 0 (impossible) and an event at 1 (certain) in your own words.

Judge a claim like 'any event with two possible outcomes has probability 1/2' — decide whether it is always true, using an example such as a biased spinner or an event much more likely than its alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a raw count of outcomes is not a probability; and 0.5 is the even-chance value only when the two outcomes are equally likely, not automatically for any two-outcome event.

constraints: The 0-to-1 probability scale is a one-dimensional magnitude; a line (physical, drawn or on screen) is the appropriate representation and no additional spatial dimension is needed.
A fixed reference line shows equivalents clearly but cannot let a child test a mis-placement, so it supports rather than replaces active placement, ordering and conversion work.

Dialogue/Socratic prompts can raise the bounds, count and even-chance-default misconceptions, but should be paired with actually placing values on a line, since placing magnitudes may be clearer when shown.

Matching and recognising equivalent forms is useful practice, but is recognition-level; include tasks where the child independently places and orders values and states a reason, not only selects from options.
Mixed-notation comparison must require conversion to a common form; do not accept ordering by surface digits or by denominator size as correct reasoning.
0.5 ('even chance') is correct only when the two outcomes are equally likely; do not teach it as the default for every two-outcome event.

Self-audit of the ordering example: 1/4 = 0.25, 0.3, 40% = 0.4 gives least-to-most order A, B, C (0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4) — correct as stated. The listed distractors (40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by digits; 1/4 largest by denominator) are intentionally wrong patterns to diagnose and must only appear as error patterns, never as correct feedback.

The assessment's die example ('probability of rolling less than 7 on a six-sided die') is certain = 1; the count answer '6' is the targeted misconception. This is logically sound and preserved as the count/bounds-confrontation idea in the Socratic activity.

The 'even chance is the default for any two-outcome event' misconception appears only in the original pedagogy field, not among the formal assessment error patterns; it has been added as a conservative Socratic probe to preserve it. This addition is an unvalidated proposal.

Legacy source claims were marked verified in the row but have not been re-checked here; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

assess.poeTask: Say: 'I'm going to roll this fair six-sided die. What is the probability that I roll a number less than 7? Write it as a number and explain — and could it be more than 1?' Have the child predict AND justify before rolling. A child who thinks in counts answers '6' (six numbers are less than 7); the correct answer is 1 (certain). Roll the die several times — every roll is under 7 — to confront the count answer: the event is certain, which is 1 on the scale, and nothing can be 'more than certain'.
probeDeeper: Where does 'even chance' sit on this line, and what is it as a decimal and a percentage?
Could a probability ever be more than 1? What would that mean?
Is 1/4 the same as, bigger than, or smaller than 0.3? How can you be sure?
Point to 0 on the line — describe an event that belongs there, and one that belongs at 1.
assess.correctAnswer: Least to most likely: A (1/4 = 0.25), then B (0.3), then C (40% = 0.4). Converting all three to the same form — decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, or positions on the line — shows the order; each sits between 0 and 1, with A a quarter of the way, B just above it, and C below the halfway point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed notations by their surface digits without converting ('40 is biggest, then 4, then 0.3')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert all three to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line) before comparing; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3
errorPatterns.distractor: C (40%), then A (1/4), then B (0.3) — 40 is the biggest number, then 4, then 0.3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by the raw numbers seen rather than their true magnitudes; may rank 1/4 above 0.3 by reading '4' as four

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction interference — a bigger denominator is read as a bigger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare their sizes
errorPatterns.distractor: A (1/4) is the most likely because it has the biggest bottom number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 1/4 high on the scale or calls it the most likely because of the 4 in the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a probability can exceed 1 or gives it as a raw count (e.g. '6' for a die)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a probability is favourable-over-total, always at most the total, so never more than 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places a mark beyond the 'certain' end, or states a probability greater than 1 or as a whole number of outcomes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place probabilities on the line or convert between notations; orders by surface digits and may put marks beyond 0 or 1
responseLevels.full: Converts freely between fraction, decimal and percentage, orders mixed-notation probabilities correctly, places each between 0 and 1, and rules out values below 0 or above 1 with a reason
responseLevels.partial: Places single-notation probabilities correctly and knows the endpoints, but slips when notations are mixed — compares by raw digits or by denominator size — or is unsure a probability cannot exceed 1

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show three events with their probabilities written in different notations: Event A has probability 1/4, Event B has probability 0.3, Event C has probability 40%. Ask the child to order them from least to most likely and to place each on a 0-to-1 line. Take the order, then ask them to explain the reason (Tier 2) — how they compared numbers written in different ways.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the scale converts to a common notation and places all three between 0 and 1; a surface reasoner ranks by the visible digits (40 > 4 > 3), and a fraction-interference reasoner treats 1/4 as large because of the 4. The Tier-2 reason — did they convert to compare? — is the separator, and only converted reasoning survives.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Complementary events
topic.description: Understand and apply the rule that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one; use this to find the probability of a complementary event (P(not A) = 1 − P(A))
evidence: Verify that probabilities of all outcomes listed for a spinner sum to 1
Calculate the probability of NOT rolling a 6 as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
Identify an error in a probability distribution where the values do not sum to 1
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a spinner has three sections and one has a probability of 0.4 and another has 0.35, can {{name}} work out the probability of landing on the third section without being told?

pedagogy.summary: Complementary events formalises two linked KS3 ideas: the probabilities of a complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1, and the complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The crux distinctive to this level is the word MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — adding probabilities (and the sum-to-1 argument) only works when outcomes cannot occur together. The classic failure is adding the probabilities of overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die, which share the number 2) and getting a nonsensical total.
bestPractices: Define mutually exclusive precisely (cannot happen at the same time) and test each situation for overlap before adding
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as the efficient route, contrasted with counting every unfavourable outcome
Use a complete outcome table / unit bar so 'exhaustive and mutually exclusive' is visible as segments filling the whole with no overlap
Expose the overlapping trap deliberately: ask for P(even or prime) on a die and show why 1/2 + 1/2 is wrong
Practise spotting invalid distributions whose probabilities don't sum to 1
keyRepresentations: Unit bar partitioned into non-overlapping outcome segments
Complete probability distribution table totalling 1
Two-circle diagram showing overlap vs no overlap (mutually exclusive or not)
P(not A) as the whole minus the A-segment
commonMisconceptions: Adding probabilities of events that are NOT mutually exclusive (overlapping events like even/prime) as though they were
Computing P(not A) by something other than 1 − P(A), or thinking P(not A) = P(A)
Assuming any list of events sums to 1 even when it is not exhaustive
Adding fractions without a common denominator when combining or complementing

learn.summary: Teach complementary events as two linked ideas: the probabilities of a complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The distinctive crux is the condition MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — adding probabilities only works when outcomes cannot occur together. Make the overlap trap explicit: even/prime on a die share the number 2, so adding 1/2 + 1/2 reaches exactly 1 and falsely suggests 'certain', when the true probability is only 5/6. Practise finding complements efficiently and rejecting distributions that do not total 1.

activities.title: Unit bar: complement and the overlap trap
feedback: If a learner says P(even or prime) = 1, ask them to list every face that is even or prime and mark any counted twice — the shared 2 reveals the overlap; counting distinct favourable outcomes gives 5/6.
If a learner computes P(not 6) by listing and miscounting, point to the whole bar minus the 6-segment: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.
Reinforce that 'even or prime' leaves out only the number 1, so the sum of 1 is misleading: the event is very likely but not certain, with true probability 5/6.
activities.rationale: A partitioned unit bar makes 'exhaustive and mutually exclusive' visible: segments filling the whole with no overlap. An overlay of overlapping events makes the double-counting of the shared 2 concrete, directly confronting the classic failure of adding non-mutually-exclusive events — insidious here because the sum lands on exactly 1 and looks valid. Live shading/overlap toggling is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism visible, not a required technology.
sourceClaims: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), but this fails for events that can occur together — e.g. rolling a 3 and a prime, or an even and a prime, share outcomes, so they are not mutually exclusive and cannot simply be added.
When events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive their probabilities total 1, so a complementary or missing probability is found by subtracting from 1 (e.g. 1 − 0.85 = 0.15).
learnerActions: Use a bar representing probability 1, divided into the six equally likely outcomes of a fair die (each 1/6).

Choose an event, e.g. 'rolling a 6'. Shade that segment, then see that P(not 6) is the whole bar minus that one segment: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. Confirm this matches the five remaining faces without counting them one by one.
Switch to overlap mode and select BOTH 'even' (2, 4, 6) and 'prime' (2, 3, 5). Shade each region on the bar.

Add P(even) = 1/2 and P(prime) = 1/2 to get 1, then compare with the bar: the arithmetic sum of the two lengths reaches the whole bar (suggesting 'certain'), yet the actual shaded union only covers five of the six segments (5/6). The extra 1/6 is the number 2, which sits in both regions and has been counted twice.
List the distinct outcomes that are even OR prime: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — five faces — so P(even or prime) = 5/6. Note that 1 is neither, so the event is NOT certain.
activities.intendedInsight: Non-overlapping segments of a complete outcome set fill the bar to exactly 1, and P(not A) is simply the rest. Adding probabilities only works when the events share no outcome; overlapping events double-count the shared outcome, so the sum overstates the true probability — here it reaches exactly 1 while the true value is only 5/6.

activities.title: Predict, roll, explain: is 'even or prime' certain?
feedback: If the prediction was 'certain', link any rolled 1 back to the claim. If no 1 came up, point out that 1 is still a possible face that is neither even nor prime: one outcome is left out, so the event cannot be certain.
Draw out that the shared outcome 2 made 1/2 + 1/2 reach 1 instead of the true 5/6; the honest count of distinct outcomes is 5/6.

Ask the probing questions: Which numbers are even OR prime, and did any appear in both sets? What is P(not even) and how did you get it? If a distribution's total came out above 1, what does that immediately tell you?
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain cycle with a real die can create a surprise if a 1 appears and the 'certain' prediction fails, which motivates the overlap check. Whatever the rolls show, listing the possible faces confirms that 1 is excluded. Spoken prediction and explanation make the reasoning audible and responsive.
sourceClaims: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), but this fails for events that can occur together — e.g. rolling a 3 and a prime, or an even and a prime, share outcomes, so they are not mutually exclusive and cannot simply be added.
learnerActions: Before rolling: 'On a fair die, is rolling a number that is even OR prime certain? Predict yes or no, give a probability, and explain your reasoning.'
Record the prediction (a learner who adds 1/2 + 1/2 will predict 'certain, probability 1').

Roll the die several times. A 1 is likely to appear but is not guaranteed in a small number of rolls (each roll has a 1/6 chance). If a 1 appears, note that it is neither even nor prime, which contradicts a 'certain' prediction. If no 1 appears, check the faces anyway: 1 is a possible outcome that is neither even nor prime, so the event still cannot be certain. Not rolling a 1 does not show the event is certain.
Revisit the reasoning: list the even-or-prime outcomes, find the double-counted 2, and correct the probability to 5/6.
Discuss: when is it safe to add two probabilities, and when is it not?
activities.intendedInsight: An outcome (1) that is neither even nor prime disproves the 'certain' claim and exposes that adding overlapping probabilities over-counts the shared outcome. Checking for a shared outcome BEFORE adding is the deciding skill.

activities.title: Sort and check: mutually exclusive or overlapping, and valid distributions
feedback: If a learner forces a non-exhaustive list to total 1, ask whether every possible outcome is included; if outcomes are missing the given probabilities need not total 1.
If a learner adds fractions without a common denominator, pause to rewrite them over a shared denominator first.
When a distribution's total exceeds 1 or falls short, treat that as an immediate signal that it cannot be a valid complete distribution.
activities.rationale: Classifying and complement-filling exercises each sub-skill — overlap detection, the complement rule, and validity of distributions — including the common error of assuming any list sums to 1. These tasks check and build fluency; they confirm classification and procedure but do not by themselves elicit an extended spoken justification.
sourceClaims: When events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive their probabilities total 1, so a complementary or missing probability is found by subtracting from 1 (e.g. 1 − 0.85 = 0.15).
learnerActions: Sort pairs of events into 'mutually exclusive' (cannot both happen) or 'overlapping' (share at least one outcome). Include die examples such as {even}/{prime} (overlap at 2), {1,2,3}/{4,5,6} (no overlap), {multiple of 3}/{even} (overlap at 6).
For each overlapping pair, list the shared outcome(s) explicitly.
Fill in complements directly: P(not 6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; P(not even) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.
Examine several probability distributions and decide which are invalid because the probabilities do not sum to 1, or because the list is not exhaustive. Explain each decision.
Verify that the probabilities listed for a given spinner sum to 1, and find any missing probability by subtracting from 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Testing for overlap is a prerequisite to adding; sum-to-1 only applies to a complete (exhaustive) set of mutually exclusive outcomes; complements are found by subtracting from 1.

constraints: Define mutually exclusive precisely (cannot happen at the same time) and test each situation for overlap before adding any probabilities.
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as the efficient route, contrasted with counting every unfavourable outcome, but ensure learners can justify why it works (the whole minus the A part).
Sum-to-1 reasoning requires the outcome set to be BOTH exhaustive and mutually exclusive; do not apply it to partial or overlapping lists.

Make clear that adding overlapping events (whose shared outcomes have nonzero probability) overstates the true probability. The incorrect sum need not exceed 1: the even/prime sum lands on exactly 1 and still misleads.
Watch for fraction errors: combining or complementing probabilities needs a common denominator.

Classification and fill-in tasks can confirm sub-skills but do not by themselves require a learner to construct a full spoken or written justification; pair them with the predict–explain activity so independent reasoning is elicited.

A fixed diagram or single overlaid example can illustrate overlap but does not let a learner test new cases themselves; use adjustable or multiple examples when the goal is for learners to discover the condition.

Self-audit confirmed: on a fair die, even = {2,4,6} and prime = {2,3,5} share only 2; their union is {2,3,4,5,6} = 5 outcomes, so P = 5/6 and 1 is the sole excluded outcome — the 'certain' claim is correctly refuted. P(not 6)=5/6 and P(not even)=1/2 are correct; {multiple of 3}={3,6} overlaps {even}={2,4,6} at 6.

A 3D treatment was judged a poor fit in the source because complement/overlap are 1D/2D partition ideas; this is a design preference, not a proven limitation, so it is not asserted as a universal law here.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: The Probability Scale
topic.description: Understand probability as a measure on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); use the language of probability including likely, unlikely, certain, and impossible
evidence: Place everyday events on a 0-to-1 probability scale with justification
Explain why a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6
Distinguish between equally likely outcomes (fair coin) and unequally likely outcomes (biased spinner)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), place events on that scale as numbers, and tell you whether a game is fair or not?

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 the probability scale is formalised: every probability is a measure from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressible as fraction, decimal or percentage, and read fluently in both directions between a described event and a numeric position. The distinctive KS3 demand is separating equally-likely situations (where P = favourable/total can be calculated) from biased ones (a loaded spinner, a drawing pin) where the scale still applies but the value cannot be got by symmetry — and refusing the equiprobability shortcut of 'n outcomes so 1/n each'.
bestPractices: Treat probability explicitly as a MEASURE on a bounded line, with 0, 1/2 and 1 as fixed landmarks and events justified by position
Contrast fair devices (calculable by favourable/total) with biased ones (a drawing pin, a bent coin) where the value must be estimated, not calculated — the scale holds either way
Confront the equiprobability shortcut directly: 'three colours' does not mean 1/3 each unless the sections are genuinely equal
Keep fraction/decimal/percentage fluency live — the same probability written three ways is one point on the line
Re-anchor the bounds: no probability is below 0 or above 1, unlike quantities in general
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 measure line with impossible / even chance / certain landmarks
Fraction = decimal = percentage triple labels on the line
Fair vs biased devices (equal spinner vs loaded spinner vs drawing pin)
Everyday-event cards placed and justified on the scale
commonMisconceptions: Equiprobability bias — assuming n possible outcomes means each has probability 1/n even when they are not equally likely (biased spinner)
Believing a probability can exceed 1 or be stated as a raw count of outcomes
Comparing probabilities written in different notations by their surface digits without converting
Assuming every probability can be CALCULATED from symmetry, with no notion that some must be estimated from data

learn.summary: KS3 learners formalise probability as a measure on a bounded 0-to-1 line: 0 = impossible, 1/2 = even chance, 1 = certain, with the same point expressible as fraction, decimal or percentage and read fluently in both directions (event → position, position → event). The distinctive demand is separating fair/equally-likely devices (where P = favourable/total can be calculated by symmetry) from biased ones (loaded spinner, bent coin, drawing pin) where symmetry no longer gives the value — it is either stated/given or, where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available, estimated from repeated data — and refusing the equiprobability shortcut 'n outcomes, so 1/n each' unless the sections/outcomes are genuinely equal. Learners also re-anchor the bounds: no probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes.

activities.title: Placing probabilities on the 0-to-1 measure line
feedback: If a learner compares 1/4 and 0.3 by surface digits, have them convert both to decimals (1/4 = 0.25) or to positions on the line; 0.25 sits below 0.3.
If a marker is pushed past the certain end, re-anchor: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1 — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, a probability cannot exceed 1.
If a probability is stated as a whole-number count of outcomes, point back to the line: a probability is a position between 0 and 1, not a tally.
activities.rationale: Treating probability explicitly as a measure on a bounded line, with 0, 1/2 and 1 as fixed landmarks and triple fraction/decimal/percentage labelling, keeps notation fluency live and makes the 0–1 bounds concrete. An optional draggable marker with a live tri-notation readout, blocked past 0 and 1, makes the mechanism vivid but is not required — a static labelled scale with tap-to-reveal triple notations works as a reference.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.
learnerActions: Work with a 0-to-1 line marked with the fixed landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain).
Place a probability of 0.7 and a probability of 1/4 at their correct positions, and read off the same point shown three ways as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
For each placement, state which landmark the event sits near and justify its position ('0.7 is above even chance, so toward the certain end').
Place a set of everyday-event cards on the scale and justify each position in words.
Test the bounds: try to place a marker beyond the certain end or below the impossible end and state why no probability can go there.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is one point on a bounded measure line; the same value can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and nothing can lie below 0 or above 1.

activities.title: Fair vs biased: when symmetry works and when it doesn't
feedback: If a learner assigns 1/3 to every colour on the biased spinner, point back to the stated 70% and the unequal sections: equal probabilities require equal sections, which this spinner does not have.

If a learner says the drawing-pin probability is 1/2 ('two ways to land'), note that the pin is not symmetric — two outcomes do not make them equally likely, and no value is stated, so it must be read off where repeated data settle.
Reinforce: P(not red) = 1 − P(red); the complement is found by subtracting from the certain bound, not by counting colours.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a calculable fair device (equal spinner, fair die) with a biased one directly confronts the equiprobability bias, and extending to a drawing pin shows a case with no symmetry and no stated value, so the probability can only be estimated. An optional sampler that runs repeated trials and lets markers approach their positions on the line makes a data-driven estimate concrete; it is a way to show the mechanism, not a mandatory tool. Note: with a finite number of trials an estimated position scatters around the true value rather than landing exactly on it.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.

The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception, and children often judge fairness arbitrarily rather than from the structure of the device (Watson & Moritz).
learnerActions: Start with a fair 3-section spinner (equal sections) and calculate each colour's probability as favourable/total — here the three colours genuinely sit at equal thirds; similarly a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6 by symmetry.
Switch to a biased spinner that is STATED to be designed so red comes up 70% of the time, with the red section much larger. Predict where the three colours sit on the line BEFORE checking.

Use the stated 70% to place red, and run or observe repeated spins to see that the three colours do not come out at equal thirds — red's observed proportion tends to sit near 0.7, above even chance and toward the certain end, while blue and yellow together share roughly the remaining 0.3 (they may be close to each other, since their split is not given); a finite run only approximates each value rather than landing on it exactly.

Place P(red) = 0.7 above even chance, toward the certain end, and work out P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3 by subtracting from 1, placing it below even chance (blue and yellow share that 0.3, and the split between them is not given).
State in words why 'three colours' did not guarantee '1/3 each' — only equal sections would.
Then consider a plain drawing pin, whose point-up probability is neither given by symmetry nor stated: decide that it can only be estimated from data, and explain why there is no symmetry to use.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal probabilities require equal sections/outcomes. For a biased device symmetry no longer gives the value: if the bias is stated you use the given value (red = 0.7); where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available (a drawing pin), the probability can only be estimated from repeated data. The scale applies in every case.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain with a real drawing pin
feedback: If the learner predicted 1/2, compare the prediction with the recorded tallies and ask what feature of the pin breaks the symmetry argument; even if the tallies happen to be near half, two possible outcomes did not justify assuming 1/2.
Stress that an estimate from 40–50 drops is approximate: more trials give a more stable position, but it will still scatter around the true value.
Connect back: this is the same point as the biased spinner — the number of possible outcomes does not fix their probabilities.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain task with a physical pin surfaces the equiprobability bias through the learner's own stated reasoning and shows that some probabilities are only knowable from data. The equiprobability bias is a documented misconception, so provoking and then confronting it is appropriate; the physical pin is a concrete way to run the trials, not evidence that touch is required to learn the idea.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception, and children often judge fairness arbitrarily rather than from the structure of the device (Watson & Moritz).
learnerActions: Before any testing, predict the probability that a dropped drawing pin lands point-up, and write down the number AND the reasoning.
Drop the pin 40–50 times, recording point-up and point-down tallies.

Compare the observed proportion to the prediction and note whether point-up and point-down came out roughly equal or clearly different; whatever the tallies show, explain why the pin's lack of symmetry means a value of 1/2 cannot simply be assumed.
Mark the estimated point-up probability on the 0-to-1 line at the position the data settle toward.
Explain what the stated-beforehand prediction revealed about the equiprobability assumption, and why this probability had to be estimated rather than calculated.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a prediction and reason before testing exposes the 'two ways to land, so even chance' assumption; because the pin is asymmetric and no value is stated, its probability must be estimated from experiment rather than assumed to be a half, and the recorded data give that estimate.

activities.title: Ordering and converting mixed-notation probabilities
feedback: If the set is ordered by visible digits, require conversion to decimals first; the surface digits mislead (1/4 looks like '4' but is 0.25).
For a 'probability = 6' or 'probability > 1' choice, re-anchor on the certain bound: a probability tops out at 1.
For the '1/3 each' claim, accept only answers that tie the equal split to equal sections, and reject it for a biased spinner.
activities.rationale: Short placement, ordering and judgement tasks drill conversion fluency, the bounds, and the equiprobability trap. These response formats can be used during teaching for practice as well as for checking; recognition or ordering items alone do not elicit the learner's own reasoning, so pair them with the explain-why prompts.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.
learnerActions: Order a mixed set such as 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely by first converting all to a common form.
Convert each probability to a decimal (or a position on the line) and check: 1/4 = 0.25, which sits below 0.3, which sits below 40% = 0.4.
Decide whether each of several statements is possible — e.g. 'a probability of 6' or 'a probability bigger than 1' — and justify using the bounds.
Judge a fair-vs-biased claim: 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3' — decide whether it is right and explain when it would and would not hold.
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities written in different notations must be converted to a common form before comparison; values cannot exceed 1 or be raw counts; '1/n each' holds only for genuinely equal sections/outcomes.

activities.title: Socratic challenges to the bounds and the 1/n shortcut
feedback: Prompt for the structural reason (section size, bounds), not just a yes/no answer.
If the learner stalls, direct them to place the value on the line and read off whether it is possible.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning can surface the bounds and equiprobability errors and push learners to justify their answers. It complements, rather than replaces, placement work: dialogue elicits reasoning while a line or device shows the placement more directly.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Could a probability be 2?' and justify the answer using the 0–1 bounds.
Respond to 'Why isn't each colour 1/3 on this biased spinner?' and explain what would have to be true for 1/3 each to hold.
Explain how you would find P(not red) from P(red), and where it sits relative to even chance.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why values cannot exceed 1 and why '1/n each' needs equal sections consolidates the two central KS3 ideas in the learner's own words.

constraints: Equal probabilities (P = favourable/total, or '1/n each') are only valid for genuinely equal sections/outcomes; do not apply symmetry to biased devices.

For asymmetric or biased devices where no value is stated (loaded spinner of unknown bias, bent coin, drawing pin) the probability cannot be got by symmetry and must be estimated from repeated data; where a bias value is stated/given (e.g. red = 70%), use the stated value directly. Any estimate from a finite number of trials is approximate and scatters around the true value.
No probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, it cannot exceed 1.
Compare probabilities by converting to a common notation (or to line positions); do not compare by surface digits.

A draggable marker, live tri-notation readout, bias/fair switch and repeated-trial sampler are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; a static labelled scale with tap-to-reveal notations is a valid reference but cannot flag a mis-placement on its own.
Recognition/ordering items can be used while teaching, but used alone they do not elicit the learner's own construction and reasoning; pair them with explain-why prompts.

Precision: the worked biased spinner is STATED to be designed at 70% red, so red = 0.7 is used from the stated value, not discovered by sampling; estimation-from-data is reserved for the drawing pin (no symmetry and no stated value). An earlier draft blurred these by saying every biased value 'must be estimated'.

evidence: Explain that getting heads on one coin flip does not change the chance of heads on the next flip
Explain why taking a red marble out of a bag and not putting it back changes the chance of drawing red next
Sort five described pairs of events into independent and dependent

topic.name: Sets & Venn Diagrams
topic.description: Enumerate sets and their unions and intersections systematically using tables, grids, and Venn diagrams to organise and count outcomes
evidence: List the elements in the union and intersection of two sets using a Venn diagram
Use a two-way table to enumerate all possible outcomes of two combined events
Shade regions of a Venn diagram to represent A ∪ B, A ∩ B, and A′ (complement)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a table or Venn diagram to systematically list all the possible outcomes of two events — like rolling two dice — and use it to count favourable outcomes?

pedagogy.summary: Sets & Venn diagrams is the procedural skill of organising and counting outcomes systematically — placing elements into the regions of a Venn diagram (or the cells of a two-way table), and reading off unions (A ∪ B), intersections (A ∩ B) and complements (A′). The crux is handling the OVERLAP correctly: elements in both sets belong only in the intersection, each element is counted once, and elements in neither set still live inside the universal set. Getting the region counts right is the foundation for all combined-event probability.
bestPractices: Fill the intersection FIRST, then subtract it from each set total so the circle-only regions are correct
Count the union by adding the distinct regions once — never |A| + |B|, which double-counts the overlap
Always account for the 'neither' region inside the universal-set rectangle; the regions must total the whole population
Use two-way tables as an alternative organiser for combined events, cross-checking against the Venn diagram
Practise shading A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′ and stating in words what each region means
keyRepresentations: Two- and three-circle Venn diagrams with a universal-set rectangle
Two-way / contingency tables for combined events
Shaded regions for union, intersection, complement
Region-count totals reconciled against the population size
commonMisconceptions: Double-counting the intersection when finding the union (writing |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|)
Writing each set's full total inside its circle without subtracting the overlap, so the diagram over-counts
Placing elements in the intersection that belong to only one set
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the regions don't total the whole population

learn.summary: Learners organise and count outcomes systematically with Venn diagrams (and two-way tables), reading off unions (A ∪ B), intersections (A ∩ B) and complements (A′). The crux is handling the overlap: elements in both sets belong only in the intersection and are counted once, while elements in neither set still live inside the universal-set rectangle and must be accounted for so all regions total the whole population.

activities.title: Build the Venn and expose the double-count
feedback: If your two counts summed to 32 (18 in football + 14 in cricket with no overlap used), the 6 who like both were counted twice — subtract one copy: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
If your union came out 32, highlight the 6 sitting in both circles: adding 18 + 14 counts them twice.
If the placed region counts add only to 26, locate the 4 students who like neither inside the rectangle: 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4, so the regions total 30.
A ∩ B = 6; A′ (not football) = cricket-only + neither = 8 + 4 = 12.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation with a visible running count is intended to make double-counting and the missing 'neither' region observable and self-checking; sorting the actual items turns the subtract-the-overlap step into something the learner works through rather than recalls.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
Organising the full sample space / set of outcomes is central to probability and frequently neglected; failing to represent all outcomes systematically underlies many probability errors.
learnerActions: Use 30 student tokens (physical or on-screen) and a two-circle Venn (A = football, B = cricket) inside a universal rectangle, with the facts: 18 like football, 14 like cricket, 6 like both.

Try the instinctive approach first: allocate 18 to the football circle and 14 to the cricket circle without using the overlap. Those two counts sum to 32 (18 + 14), yet only 30 students exist — on screen a counter reads 32, while with physical tokens you run out before finishing the cricket circle. Either outcome shows that some students are being counted twice — here, the 6 'both' students. Note that the excess of 2 (32 − 30) is not the size of the overlap, because 4 students like neither sport.
Move the 6 'both' students into the overlap region, then adjust so each circle's own-only region reads 12 (18 − 6) and 8 (14 − 6).
Place the 4 left-over students in the 'neither' region inside the rectangle, and check the regions total 30.
State the union count by adding the distinct regions once: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
Shade and state in words what each region means for A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′.
activities.intendedInsight: Elements in both sets are counted twice if you compute |A| + |B|; filling the intersection first and subtracting it from each total gives the correct circle-only regions, and the 'neither' region must be included so everything totals the population.

activities.title: Classify, count, and cross-check with a two-way table
feedback: If you chose 32 as the union, that adds both set totals and counts the 6 shared students twice; the union is 26.
If the table and the diagram disagree, re-check which cell the 'both' and the 'neither' groups belong in — the two totals must match.
The row and column totals of the two-way table should reconcile to the whole population of 30.
activities.rationale: Classification exercises the enumeration and the double-counting trap, and the two-way table gives a second representation that can catch miscounts the diagram alone might hide; it checks and drills classification but does not itself elicit free shading or diagram construction.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
Organising the full sample space / set of outcomes is central to probability and frequently neglected; failing to represent all outcomes systematically underlies many probability errors.
learnerActions: Sort each element into its correct Venn region (football-only, cricket-only, both, or neither).
Decide which count is the union of A and B, distinguishing the correct 26 from the double-counted 32.
Give the 'neither' count by reconciling against the total of 30.
Re-represent the same combined events in a two-way / contingency table and check the cell totals match the Venn region counts.
activities.intendedInsight: A two-way table is an alternative organiser for combined events; cross-checking it against the Venn diagram confirms every outcome is counted exactly once.

activities.title: Read the regions: tap-to-reveal reference
feedback: Confirm that A′ means everything not in A — which here includes both cricket-only and the 'neither' region.
Check that A ∩ B is the overlap only, not either whole circle.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal reference can teach the layout and notation; it is a scaffold because it does not let the learner build a diagram or test a miscount, so pair it with the construction activity.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
learnerActions: Study a labelled Venn diagram and tap each region or shaded set to reveal its set notation (for example A ∩ B, or A ∪ B and A′, which are each made of more than one region), its plain-language meaning, and its count.
Match each shaded picture to its correct name and verbal description before building your own diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the layout and the meaning of each shaded region supports accurate building and counting.

activities.title: Socratic overlap check
feedback: If the learner says 18 + 14, prompt them to find the 6 counted in both and subtract one copy to get 26.
If they omit the 'neither' group, ask what 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) tells them.
activities.rationale: Targeted questioning can surface the subtract-the-overlap and 'neither' errors; learners should still carry out the placement and counting themselves, so use dialogue alongside construction rather than instead of it.
learnerActions: Work through prompts such as 'Does the 18 include the 6 who like both, or not?' and explain your reasoning.
Answer 'How many like football OR cricket, and why isn't it simply 18 + 14?' in your own words.
Explain where the students who like neither go and how many there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why the overlap must be subtracted once, and why the 'neither' group still sits inside the universal set, consolidates the enumeration logic.

constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract it from each set total so the circle-only regions are correct.
Count the union as |A unionB|=|A|+|B|-|A intersectionB|. Subtract the overlap once; if it is zero, direct addition is valid. In this example the union is18+14-6=26.
Always account for the 'neither' region inside the universal-set rectangle; the regions must total the whole population (30 here).
Tap-to-reveal and read-only diagrams teach layout and notation but do not let the learner build a diagram or test a miscount; use them as scaffolds alongside hands-on construction.
Choice/classification steps drill enumeration and the double-count trap but do not elicit free shading or independent diagram construction; pair them with a build/shade task.
Socratic dialogue can surface overlap and 'neither' errors, but learners should still do the placement and counting themselves.
The '32' (18 + 14) and '38' (football-only 18 + overlap 6 + cricket-only 14) figures are learner error patterns only and must never be offered as valid counts; the correct union is 26.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 18 − 6 = 12, 14 − 6 = 8, union 12 + 6 + 8 = 26, neither 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4, and A′ = 8 + 4 = 12. The '32' figure (18 + 14) is retained only as the double-counted error to be corrected; the '38' figure (18 + 6 + 14 when full totals are placed plus a separate overlap) is likewise an error pattern only, not restated as a learner-facing count.

With 30 literal physical tokens a learner cannot place 32; the '32' is reframed as the arithmetic sum of the two attempted counts (on screen a counter reads 32; with physical tokens you run out), so the scenario stays coherent across both modalities.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' for this 2D organising task; this has not been propagated as a universal law. A 3D interaction is simply not proposed because the task is a 2D sorting/counting task, not because 3D is incapable of teaching.

Live counters, draggable tokens, and a shading tool are retained as concrete, optional interaction examples that may make the counting mechanism visible, not as mandatory mechanisms; physical tokens on paper can serve the same purpose.
Efficacy phrasing ('self-checking', 'visible', 'observable') reflects design intent inherited from the original rationale and is not independently validated.

probeDeeper: You wrote 18 in the football circle — does that include the 6 who like both, or not?
How many like football OR cricket? Why isn't it simply 18 + 14?
Where do the students who like neither sport go, and how many are there?
Shade 'likes cricket but not football' — which region is that, and what's the count?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: 6 in the intersection, 12 in football-only (18 − 6), 8 in cricket-only (14 − 6), and 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4 outside both circles. A ∪ B = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26 (not 18 + 14 = 32). A ∩ B = 6. A′ (not football) = cricket-only + neither = 8 + 4 = 12. Regions are filled by subtracting the overlap, the union is counted once, and the 'neither' region is included.

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the union as 32 by adding the two set totals without removing the shared 6

errorPatterns.nextMove: Fill the intersection first, then subtract it from each total to get the circle-only regions (12 and 8) before anything else

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this and paper: 'In a class of 30, 18 students like football, 14 like cricket, and 6 like both. Draw a two-circle Venn diagram and fill in the numbers. (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they subtract the 6 from each circle, whether the union double-counts the overlap, and whether they place the students who like neither.)
