topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Tree diagrams
topic.description: Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events using listing, tables, and tree diagrams, and calculate theoretical probabilities as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes
evidence: List all 36 outcomes when rolling two dice and find P(total = 7)
Draw a tree diagram for two successive events and multiply along branches for combined probabilities
Calculate the probability of a combined event using a sample space diagram and simplify the fraction
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a tree diagram to map out all possible outcomes of a two-step probability situation — like flipping a coin and then rolling a die — and calculate the probability of any particular combination?

pedagogy.summary: Tree diagrams (and sample-space grids and systematic listing) generate the full set of equally-likely outcomes for single and combined events, from which theoretical probability is favourable ÷ total. Students list outcomes (e.g. the 36 ordered results of two dice), draw trees with probabilities on the branches, MULTIPLY along a path (the AND rule) and ADD across paths (the OR rule), and adjust probabilities for without-replacement (dependent) events. The recurring conceptual hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — like the eleven dice totals — are equally likely.
bestPractices: Build the complete sample space first (grid or list), respecting ORDER, so favourable/total rests on genuinely equally-likely outcomes
Confront the two-dice trap head-on: the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT equally likely; there are 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes
Teach the AND rule (multiply along a branch) and OR rule (add across paths) explicitly, and the complement shortcut for 'at least one'
For without-replacement problems, recompute the second-level branch probabilities from the reduced situation (dependent events)
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so common denominators are available for adding paths
keyRepresentations: Sample-space grid / two-way table (e.g. 6×6 for two dice)
Systematic ordered listing of outcomes
Probability tree with values on branches; multiply along, add across
Reduced-denominator second branches for dependent events
commonMisconceptions: Assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treating the eleven totals of two dice as each 1/11 (equiprobability bias)
Ignoring order when listing — counting 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, undercounting the sample space
Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplying AND/OR)
Reusing the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event

learn.summary: Students build complete, equally-likely sample spaces (ordered lists or grids) for single and combined events, then compute theoretical probability as favourable ÷ total. They draw probability trees, multiply along a single path (AND), add across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths (OR), use the complement for 'at least one', and recompute second-level branches for without-replacement (dependent) events. The central hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — such as the eleven dice totals — are equally likely, when it is the 36 ordered outcomes that are equally likely.

activities.title: The two-dice grid: why totals are not equally likely
feedback: If a learner writes P(7) = 1/11: there are eleven possible totals, but they do not occur equally often. Count the shaded cells — seven has six ways, two has just one — so the totals cannot each be 1/11.

If a learner counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome (getting three ways to make 7, or 21 outcomes total): treat the dice as an ordered pair, first then second; (3,4) and (4,3) are genuinely different results, giving 36 outcomes and six ways to make 7.
Confirm success when the full grid is filled, six cells are identified for total 7, and the learner can say the ordered outcomes — not the totals — are what is equally likely.
activities.rationale: Theoretical probability only equals favourable ÷ total when the counted outcomes are genuinely equally likely; the two-dice grid makes the distinction between elemental equally-likely outcomes and aggregated events visible and countable.
sourceClaims: Children (and adults) show an equiprobability bias in the two-dice problem, assuming all the possible totals are equally probable; the difficulty is distinguishing elemental equally-likely outcomes from aggregated events, which requires representing the full sample space.
learnerActions: On paper or a 6×6 grid, write the total in every one of the 36 cells for (first die, second die), keeping the two dice as an ordered pair so 3+4 and 4+3 are separate cells.
Shade all cells where the total is 7 and count them (6 cells: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1), then shade cells where the total is 2 (1 cell: 1+1).
State P(total = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(total = 2) = 1/36.
Explain in a sentence why P(7) is NOT 1/11, referring to the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: The 36 ordered (die1, die2) outcomes are equally likely; the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT, because different totals arise from different numbers of ordered outcomes.

activities.title: Trees: multiply along a path, add across paths
feedback: If a learner computes P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6: along a single path use the AND rule and multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12). Adding is only for OR across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths.
If a learner cancels fractions early and then struggles to add paths: keep denominators uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.
Confirm success when the learner multiplies along a path for a combined event and adds across separate paths for an 'or' event, and can say which operation goes with AND and which with OR.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating multiply-along (AND) from add-across (OR) addresses the common error of applying the wrong operation, and delaying cancellation keeps path addition tractable.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Draw a probability tree for a coin flip followed by a die roll, writing the probability on each branch and checking each set of branches sums to 1.
Find P(tail and 6) by multiplying along the single path: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
Find a two-path 'OR' probability by computing each separate complete path's product, then adding the path products together (the paths are mutually exclusive, so adding is valid).
Leave fractions uncancelled until the final step so paths share common denominators when added.
activities.intendedInsight: Along one path, combined events use AND and you multiply; across separate complete paths that each satisfy the question, you use OR and add. These are different operations for different situations.

activities.title: Without replacement: the second branch changes
feedback: If a learner keeps the original probabilities on the second branches: after removing a counter there are fewer counters in total and one fewer of the colour drawn — recompute each second branch from what is actually left.
Confirm success when every second-level branch reflects the reduced totals and the path product uses those updated values.
activities.rationale: Recomputing second-level branches from the reduced situation is the core procedure for dependent events and directly targets the misconception of reusing first-event probabilities.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Set up a bag problem, e.g. 3 red and 2 blue counters, and draw a tree for taking two counters without replacing the first.

Write the first-draw probabilities (3/5 red, 2/5 blue), then recompute each second-draw branch from the reduced situation — one fewer counter in total, and one fewer of whatever was drawn (e.g. after a red: 2/4 red, 2/4 blue).

If an optional tool offers a 'replace / don't replace' switch, toggle it and watch the second-level branch probabilities change (with no replacement) or stay the same (with replacement) to see the dependency.
Find a combined probability, e.g. P(two reds) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, multiplying along the path with the updated second branch.
activities.intendedInsight: For dependent (without-replacement) events, the second draw's probabilities depend on the first outcome, so they must be recomputed from the reduced contents rather than reused.

activities.title: Drill and check: rules and the equiprobability trap
feedback: For the P(7) item, 1/11 is incorrect: counting ordered outcomes gives 6/36 = 1/6; 1/11 wrongly assumes the eleven totals are equally likely.
For the fill-in, the AND rule gives 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
For the without-replacement item, the second branch uses the reduced totals; keeping the original values is the error to catch.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition and fill-in items reinforce the rules and surface the equiprobability distractor; they consolidate procedures but do not by themselves require constructing a full fresh sample space, so they supplement — and do not replace — the construction activities. Efficacy of the format is proposed, not demonstrated.
learnerActions: Answer a short-answer item: P(total = 7) with two dice — write the fraction and justify it, explaining why the common answer 1/11 is wrong.
Complete a fill-in: P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × ___ = ___.
Solve a without-replacement item where the second branch must be recomputed, and explain why it differs from the first.
Where available, tap grid cells to reveal their totals or tap a tree path to reveal its product, using these only to self-check after you have reasoned.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick recognition and fill-in checks can reinforce the AND/OR rules and resurface the equiprobability trap, but learners should reason first and use any reveal only to confirm; such items check and consolidate the procedures and do not by themselves build a full fresh sample space.

constraints: Sample spaces must be built on genuinely equally-likely outcomes; for two dice that means the 36 ordered (die1, die2) pairs, not the eleven totals.
Order must be respected when listing: (3,4) and (4,3) are distinct outcomes; ignoring order undercounts the sample space.
For dependent (without-replacement) events, every second-level branch must be recomputed from the reduced contents; first-event probabilities cannot be reused.
The OR (add-across) rule applies only to separate, mutually exclusive complete paths; the AND (multiply-along) rule applies within a single path.
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.

Short-answer, fill-in and tap-to-reveal items can reinforce and self-check the rules, but do not require a learner to independently construct a complete fresh sample space; pair them with construction tasks.

Tap-to-reveal grids/trees and a replace/don't-replace toggle are optional supports to make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and should be used after the learner has reasoned, not instead of reasoning.
Rolling physical or 3D dice can add realism and generate data, but the counting and branch arithmetic are carried by the grid and tree; feed any physical results back into the grid/tree.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: two-dice total 7 has six ordered ways (1+6,2+5,3+4,4+3,5+2,6+1) → 6/36 = 1/6; total 2 has one way (1+1) → 1/36; P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12; without-replacement example P(two reds from 3R,2B) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10 (first draw 3/5 red, 2/5 blue). All consistent with the source row.
The '1/11' value appears only as a misconception to be corrected, never as a valid answer offered to learners.
The complement shortcut for 'at least one' is named in the pedagogy summary but is not given a worked activity here; a reviewer may wish to add one.

Source claims cited support the underlying principles (tree rules; equiprobability bias) but do not establish that these specific activities or any particular interactive/toggle/tap-to-reveal feature were tested for efficacy; efficacy of any medium is therefore left as proposed/intended, not demonstrated.

probeDeeper: You flip a coin AND roll a die — what is P(heads and a 6)? Do you add or multiply the branch probabilities, and why?
Are the totals 2 to 12 equally likely? How many ways can you make 7, and how many ways to make 2?
If you draw two counters from a bag WITHOUT replacing the first, do the second-branch probabilities stay the same? Why not?
Why is 3+4 counted separately from 4+3 in the grid?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: builds the sample space of 36 equally-likely ordered (die1, die2) outcomes — via a grid or systematic list — finds 6 ways to total 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) giving P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, and 1 way to total 2 (1+1) giving P(2) = 1/36. The student recognises the 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely but the totals are not.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the 6×6 grid of the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes; count how many make each total — seven has six ways, two has one — so the totals are not equally likely
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(7) = 1/11 (or P(2) = 1/11) without building the sample space of ordered outcomes

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores order when listing, undercounting the sample space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat (die1, die2) as ordered pairs — 3+4 and 4+3 are different cells on the grid; there are 36 outcomes, six of which total 7
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, giving 21 outcomes or only three ways to make 7

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplies the AND rule)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Along a single path use the AND rule: multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12); adding is for OR across separate paths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up combined event computes P(A and B) as P(A) + P(B) — e.g. P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6

errorPatterns.pattern: Reuses the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event
errorPatterns.nextMove: For dependent events recompute the second branch from the reduced situation — one fewer item, and one fewer of whatever was drawn
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a 'draw two without replacing' probe, keeps the original probabilities on the second set of branches

responseLevels.gap: Assumes the totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11); no systematic sample space; adds branch probabilities for combined events
responseLevels.full: Builds the complete 36-outcome ordered sample space, counts favourable outcomes correctly (6 ways to 7 → 1/6), multiplies along branches and adds across paths, and recomputes probabilities for without-replacement events
responseLevels.partial: Builds some of the sample space and multiplies along branches for simple independent cases, but undercounts by ignoring order, or keeps probabilities fixed for without-replacement events — computes without a complete, ordered sample space

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child paper and this task: 'Two fair dice are rolled and the two numbers are added together. Work out the probability the total is 7. Then work out the probability the total is 2.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they treat all totals 2–12 as equally likely or systematically build the 36-outcome sample space, whether they respect order when counting the ways to make 7, and how they express and simplify the answers.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the student who lays out all 36 ordered outcomes and counts six ways to make 7 from one who assumes the eleven totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11), or ignores order and undercounts (three ways to 7, or 21 outcomes). The two-dice sample space is the classic exposer of assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely.

sources.claim: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.

sources.claim: Children (and adults) show an equiprobability bias in the two-dice problem, assuming all the possible totals are equally probable; the difficulty is distinguishing elemental equally-likely outcomes from aggregated events, which requires representing the full sample space.

topic.name: Venn Diagrams and Counting Outcomes
topic.description: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets to organise and count outcomes; use systematic listing and the product rule for counting to enumerate all possible outcomes of combined events
evidence: Draw a two-circle Venn diagram to sort 30 students by whether they like football, like cricket, or like both
Shade the intersection A ∩ B and the union A ∪ B on a Venn diagram and explain what each region represents
Use a completed Venn diagram to calculate P(A), P(B), P(A ∩ B), and P(A ∪ B)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} surveys a class about which sports they play and draws a Venn diagram to show the results, can they use it to find out how many students play both sports — and calculate the probability of picking one of those students at random?

pedagogy.summary: Venn diagrams organise outcomes into regions defined by set membership: elements outside both circles, in one circle only, and in the overlap (intersection). Students learn to CONSTRUCT the diagram (fill the intersection FIRST, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' universal-set remainder) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). The intersection A∩B is 'in both', the union A∪B is 'in either', and probability is always the region count over the total number in the universal set (unless a conditional restricts the denominator). Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set that the diagram then organises.
bestPractices: Fill the INTERSECTION first, then subtract it from each set total to get the 'only-A' and 'only-B' regions — this prevents double-counting the overlap
Always place the 'neither' elements inside the rectangle (universal set) but outside both circles, and check all regions sum to the total
Name each region in words before writing set notation — 'likes both', 'likes cricket but not football' — then attach A∩B, A∪B, A only
Compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; only restrict the denominator when the question conditions on a subset
Use systematic listing / the product rule to build the complete outcome set, then sort it into the diagram so favourable ÷ total rests on genuine outcomes
keyRepresentations: Two-circle Venn diagram inside a labelled rectangle (universal set)
Three-circle Venn diagram for three-set problems (seven internal regions)
Intersection-first fill order: overlap, then 'only' regions by subtraction, then 'neither'
Two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions
commonMisconceptions: Confusing intersection and union — shading 'in either' when asked for 'in both', or vice versa
Double-counting the overlap — adding the two circle totals for A∪B without subtracting A∩B
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the diagram's regions do not sum to the universal-set total
Using a circle total (or the whole universal set) as the denominator for a probability that is actually conditional on a restricted subset

learn.summary: Students learn to CONSTRUCT a Venn diagram (fill the intersection first, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' remainder inside the universal-set rectangle) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). A∩B is 'in both', A∪B is 'in either', and probability is region-count over the universal-set total unless a conditional restricts the denominator. Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set the diagram then organises. The discriminating skill is construction on a fresh case, which exposes intersection/union confusion and wrong-denominator errors that reading a pre-labelled diagram can hide.

activities.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities
feedback: If a learner shades both whole circles for A∪B, point out the overlap has been counted twice and the running total passes 30 — the middle six can only be counted once, so the union count is A + B − A∩B.

If they shade the entire cricket circle (14) for 'cricket but NOT football', return to region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — the crescent only (8).
If they write P(cricket only) = 8/14, ask 'out of how many students altogether?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30, so 8/30.
If they answer 'the probability is 8' (a count), restate that a probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the total: 8 out of 30 is 8/30.
On the conditional, if they keep 30 as the denominator, ask who is being considered now — only the cricket-lovers, so the denominator is 14, not 30.
activities.rationale: Venn regions are spatial partitions of the outcome set; constructing the diagram from raw data (intersection-first, then subtraction, then 'neither') prevents double-counting and makes the correct denominator concrete. Construction on a fresh description is the move that distinguishes genuine understanding from parroting region labels.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Place 30 student tokens into a two-circle Venn (football / cricket) inside a rectangle; fill the intersection first (likes both), then the 'only' crescents (by subtracting the overlap from each set total when only totals are given), then the 'neither' region outside both circles — e.g. 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither.
Check that all regions sum to 30 before reading anything off.
Name each region in words BEFORE writing notation: 'likes both' = A∩B, 'football only' = A only, 'likes either' = A∪B, 'neither' outside both.
Shade 'likes cricket but NOT football' (the cricket-only crescent, 8 students) and write its probability as 8/30 = 4/15 over the total of 30.
Shade A∪B and find its COUNT two ways: by adding region counts (12 + 6 + 8 = 26), and by checking 18 + 14 − 6 = 26 to see why the overlap is subtracted; the probability is then 26/30.
Switch to a conditional: 'among the cricket-lovers, what fraction also like football?' — identify the new denominator (14, all who like cricket) and compute 6/14.
activities.intendedInsight: The overlap counts once, so the union COUNT is A + B − A∩B; and the denominator is the whole universal set unless a question conditions on a restricted subset, in which case the denominator shrinks to that subset.

activities.title: Generate the full outcome set, then sort it into the diagram
feedback: If a probability looks wrong, check whether every outcome was listed — a missing outcome changes both the region count and the total.

If the learner struggles to coordinate regions with individual outcomes, have them tag each listed outcome with its region before counting, so region totals are built from real outcomes rather than guessed.
activities.rationale: Research highlights that children's core difficulty is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes; building the outcome set first and sorting it addresses that directly.
sourceClaims: Correctly enumerating and counting outcomes over unions and intersections requires representing the complete set of outcomes systematically (tables, grids, Venn diagrams); the difficulty children face is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes.
learnerActions: For a combined-events scenario, use systematic listing or the product rule to enumerate every possible outcome before sorting.
Place each enumerated outcome into the correct Venn region (or a two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions).

Confirm that favourable ÷ total rests on the genuine, fully-listed outcomes, and that those listed outcomes are equally likely (e.g. ordered pairs from a fair coin and a fair die, not just the possible totals of two dice). Then count the region, count the universal set and form the fraction.
Compare the Venn diagram and a two-way table of the same data to see that both encode the four regions (both, A only, B only, neither).
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities read off a diagram are only trustworthy when the complete set of equally likely outcomes has been enumerated and sorted correctly; the diagram organises outcomes but does not create them.

activities.title: Explain why the overlap is not counted twice (reasoning talk)
feedback: If a learner adds the two circle totals for the union, ask them to point to who gets counted twice and why that inflates the total.
If they say adding 'neither' students changes no probabilities, remind them the universal-set total grew, so every probability over the whole set changes even though the circle counts did not.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can probe why the overlap is not double-counted and why denominators shift, but the core skill is constructing and reading the spatial diagram, so talk is best used alongside construction, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Justify each region count aloud: how many like football altogether (18, not 12), how many like cricket altogether (14), how many like both (6).

Explain in your own words why the number who like football OR cricket is 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 — and NOT 18 + 14 = 32 — because the 6 who like both are already included in each circle total; the probability is then 26/30.

State what changes and what stays the same if four more 'neither' students join: the universal-set total rises to 34, so every probability taken over the universal set changes, while the region counts for football and cricket stay fixed (and a probability taken only among cricket-lovers, like 6/14, is unaffected).
activities.intendedInsight: Verbal justification surfaces the double-counting logic and the role of the denominator, reinforcing the construction skill rather than replacing it.

activities.title: Interpretation and sorting practice (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner selects 6/18, ask what the denominator should be — the universal-set total of 30, not a circle total.
If they select the bare count 6, restate that a probability is a fraction of the total: 6/30.
activities.rationale: Tap-to-reveal and sorting tasks teach the region vocabulary and interpretation efficiently, but they are recognition-level: they do not require the learner to construct a diagram from raw data or decide a denominator on a fresh case. Use them before, not instead of, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: On a pre-authored Venn, reveal region labels: tap the overlap for 'likes both — 6 students — A∩B', a circle-only crescent for 'football only — 12', outside for 'neither — 4'; answer 'What fraction like both?' → 6/30.
Sort described students into the four regions (drag-to-region sorting).
Match region names (A∩B, A∪B, A only) to shaded pictures.
Read a probability off a completed diagram, watching for a wrong-denominator option such as 6/18 (circle-total denominator) or an unnormalised count such as 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising region meanings and reading probabilities off a completed diagram builds the vocabulary that construction then applies.

constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract to get the 'only' regions, then place 'neither' inside the rectangle but outside both circles — and check all regions sum to the universal-set total.

When one member of the universal set is chosen at random (each equally likely), compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; restrict the denominator only when the question conditions on a subset.
Keep probabilities and counts distinct: a union COUNT may exceed 1 (e.g. 26), but the probability is that count over the total (26/30) and always lies between 0 and 1.

Recognition and sorting tasks (tap-to-reveal, matching, categorization, multiple choice) assess and build vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a diagram from raw data or an independently chosen denominator; keep a genuine construct-from-description task in the sequence.
A completed/pre-authored Venn is a scaffold: it teaches what each region means but cannot test whether the learner can build a diagram or choose the correct denominator on a new case.

Interactive features (drag tokens into regions, tap-to-shade with live set-notation and probability recompute, a conditional mode that greys out the rest and switches the denominator, a flag when the union overlap is selected twice) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required.
A two-way table is a valid alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions; do not treat the circle layout as the only representation.
Three-circle Venn diagrams (seven internal regions) extend the same logic for three-set problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic on the worked example (30 students: 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither): football total 12+6=18, cricket total 8+6=14, union 12+8+6=26 = 18+14−6, neither 4, grand total 18+8+4=30 (or 12+6+8+4=30) — all consistent. P(cricket only)=8/30=4/15 and P(both)=6/30=1/5 check out. The conditional P(football | cricket)=6/14 uses denominator 14 (all cricket-lovers), which is correct.

The union work distinguishes the union COUNT (26) from its probability (26/30). The original assessment probe ('What is P(likes football OR cricket)? ... do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14?') had conflated the count with the probability; this is kept distinct in the learner-facing actions.

The original source row claimed a 3D representation 'adds nothing' to a flat categorical partition. This is a catalog-style universal claim not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than propagated. A flat partition is well-suited here without asserting a third dimension is universally useless.
The original also framed dialogue as something 'talk alone cannot deliver'; rescoped to a narrow point that verbal justification complements, rather than replaces, construction.
Original assessment distractor '6/18' uses a circle-total denominator (football total 18); retained as a diagnostic distractor, not as a valid answer.

The Bryant & Nunes claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims (it supports the systematic-enumeration principle of Activity 2, not Activity 1's construction/double-counting principle) and retained where it directly applies.

probeDeeper: You said the middle is 6 — if I ask how many like football ALTOGETHER, is it 12 or 18? Why?
What is P(likes football OR cricket)? Talk me through it — do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14? Why can't you just add the two circle totals?
Suppose I only look at the students who like cricket — among THEM, what fraction also like football? What's the denominator now, and why did it change?
If four more students who like neither sport joined, which probabilities would change and which would stay the same?
assess.correctAnswer: Tier 1 (interpret): the middle region is the intersection — students who like both football AND cricket — 6 students, so P(both) = 6/30 = 1/5. Tier 2 (construct): shades ONLY the cricket-only crescent (the part of the cricket circle outside the overlap), 8 students, and writes P = 8/30 = 4/15 over the universal-set total of 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses intersection and union when shading — shades the whole cricket circle (overlap included) for 'cricket but NOT football', or the reverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to region-by-region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — shade the crescent only
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the construct move, shades the entire cricket circle (14) rather than the cricket-only crescent (8), or shades the overlap when 'only' was asked

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a wrong denominator — divides by a circle total (or, for a conditional, by the whole universal set) instead of the total in the correct set
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'out of how many?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30; only a conditional ('among cricket-lovers') restricts the denominator to that subset
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes P(cricket only) = 8/14 (cricket-circle denominator) instead of 8/30, or on a conditional keeps 30 as the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports a region frequency as the probability — writes P = 8 or P = 6, not a fraction of the total
errorPatterns.nextMove: A probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the universal-set total; 8 students out of 30 means 8/30
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'the probability is 8' or 'the probability is 6', giving a count rather than count/total

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the overlap as 'both', shades union when intersection is asked, or reports counts instead of probabilities; construction fails
responseLevels.full: Constructs the region accurately (cricket-only crescent), writes the probability over the correct denominator (8/30 = 4/15), computes A∪B by subtracting the double-counted overlap, and shifts the denominator correctly when a question is conditional — transferring the region logic to a new description
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a labelled diagram correctly and reads P(both) off it, but the construct move slips — shades the whole circle for a 'not' region, or uses a circle total as the denominator; can name regions but cannot yet coordinate 'only', union, and the correct denominator on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a completed two-circle Venn inside a rectangle: 12 in 'football only', 6 in the overlap, 8 in 'cricket only', 4 outside both (30 students total). FIRST ask: 'Point to the middle region — what does it mean, and how many students like BOTH sports? What is the probability a random student likes both?' THEN hand them a blank Venn and this fresh description and ask them to CONSTRUCT it and answer: 'Shade the region for students who like cricket but NOT football, and write the probability as a fraction.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a given region is easier than constructing one: a child can parrot 'the middle is both' yet still shade the whole cricket circle (including the overlap) for 'cricket but NOT football', or divide by a circle total instead of 30. The construct move is the discriminator — it exposes intersection/union confusion and denominator errors that reading a labelled diagram hides.
